title: BASIS FOR THE PREPARATION OF THE SUSTAINABILITY STATEMENT [BP-1, BP-2]
heading: BASIS FOR THE PREPARATION OF THE SUSTAINABILITY STATEMENT [BP-1, BP-2]
start_phrase: The information, data and ratios and statements contained in the statement relate to the PKO Bank Polski S.A Group, i.e. the parent company PKO Bank Polski S.A together with its consolidated subsidiaries, unless otherwise indicated.
summary:
- Capital markets activities:
  - Variable-rate bond issue with quarterly payments rated A3 by Moody’s, admitted to trading on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange; intention to list also on the regulated market in Warsaw.
  - PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A. issued series 15 mortgage covered bonds: PLN 800 million, issue date 27 Feb 2025, maturity 27 Feb 2029, floating 3M WIBOR + 0.80 bps.

- Significant post–balance sheet events (2025):
  - 30 Jan: Annex to an unfunded credit protection guarantee (CRR) for a Group corporate credit portfolio. Total portfolio PLN 16,886 million: Portfolio A (bonds) PLN 2,365 million at 100% coverage; Portfolio B (other receivables) PLN 14,521 million at 80% coverage; maximum guarantee amount unchanged at PLN 13,982 million.
  - 14 Feb: BSafer sp. z o.o. (a PKO VC-fizan joint venture within the Group) filed for bankruptcy due to insolvency.

- Sustainability Statement for 2024 – scope and methodology:
  - Applies to PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group (parent plus 36 consolidated subsidiaries as at 31 Dec 2024), with consolidation scope aligned to the 2024 consolidated financial statements.
  - Only the parent bank is legally obliged to report for 2024, but disclosures cover the Group’s value chain (upstream and downstream), Scope 3 GHG emissions, and consumer/end-user matters.
  - No omission of information related to intellectual property, know-how, innovation, or withholding of information on upcoming events/negotiations.
  - Policies are presented on a consolidated basis; where no Group policy exists, the Bank’s policy is presented; subsidiaries’ own policies are not detailed as no subsidiary reported entity-specific impacts/risks/opportunities or separate reporting obligations. Objectives are disclosed where defined at Group level.
  - Governance of policies: adopted by Management Board; procedures/principles/decisions specify implementing organizational levels; no exclusions unless explicitly stated.
  - Reporting period 1 Jan–31 Dec 2024; no indicators with high measurement uncertainty; indicators attested only through the sustainability statement attestation; no cross-referencing to other report sections.

- Governance structure and composition:
  - Management Board: 7 executives (6 men, 1 woman); women’s share 17% at year-end (average 11% in 2024). Clear division of responsibilities across strategy, internal audit, security, compliance/conduct/reputation risk, legal, HR, communications/marketing, corporate governance; retail and corporate banking (retail products, investment/insurance offering design, sales/service to individuals and companies); corporate and investment banking (investment banking, custody, treasury products, corporate/public sector client offering and sales); finance and accounting (macroeconomics, planning/controlling, accounting/reporting, tax, sustainability); administration (property, procurement); operations and international banking (operations, customer advocacy, international/institutional clients, remote channels, product administration, cash management); technology (IT); risk management (all risks except compliance/conduct/reputation; restructuring and recovery).
  - Competency and suitability: periodic individual and collective assessments; PFSA approval required for the President and the risk-management Board member.
  - Supervisory Board: 8 non-executive, all independent; women’s share 33% at year-end (average 47% in 2024). Members meet qualifications for companies with State Treasury participation; backgrounds in academia, business, and audit-advisory, with extensive supervisory and senior banking/audit experience.
text:
The information, data and ratios and statements contained in the statement relate to the PKO Bank Polski S.A Group, 
i.e. the parent company PKO Bank Polski S.A together with its consolidated subsidiaries, unless otherwise indicated. 
As at 31 December 2024 the Bank’s Group comprised PKO Bank Polski S.A. as the parent and 36 direct or indirect 
subsidiaries (at all levels). The scope of consolidation in this report is the same as for the consolidated financial 
statements for 2024. In the Bank’s Group, only the  Bank is subject to the obligation to report on sustainable 
development for the year 2024. The report applies to the value chain at both the higher and lower levels (upstream 
and downstream) in the context of describing the value chain of the Bank's Group,  data on greenhouse gas emissions 
in scope 3, and in relation to issues concerning consumers and end -users. The Bank's Group does not utilize the 
option of omitting information related to intellectual property, know -how, or innovation effects, nor does it use the 
option to withhold information about upcoming events or matters under negotiation.  
The Bank’s Group presents its policies on a consolidated basis. In the absence of group policies, the Bank's policies 
are presented, which should serve as a startin g point for the future development of regulations at the Group level or 
have been transferred to subsidiaries for implementation. The policies of the subsidiaries, where no Group policy 
exists, are not described, as none of the subsidiaries reported any im pact, risk, or opportunity (IRO) specific to their 
entity, nor are any of them subject to the obligation to report on sustainable development for the year 2024, which 
would be carried out through disclosure at the parent company level. The objectives are r eported for policies at the 
Group level, provided they have been defined.  
The policies adopted by the Management Board Resolution include its responsibility for their implementation. In the 
case of the Procedures, Principles, and Decisions, the level at w hich they were adopted is indicated, meaning 
specifying the organizational level responsible for their implementation. Policies and internal regulations do not apply 
exclusions unless specified otherwise.  
This report is prepared annually and includes infor mation and data for the period from 1 January to 31 December 
2024. No indicators with a high level of measurement uncertainty were identified. The disclosed indicators have not 
undergone any attestation processes other than the attestation of the sustainab le development statement.  
The Group does not identify information included by reference to other parts of the Directors’ Report.  THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP  
DIRECTOR’S REPORT FOR 2024  
prepared jointly with the PKO Bank Polski S.A Director’s Report   
 
 Strona 170/288

title: THE ROLE OF THE ADMINISTRATIVE, MANAGEMENT AND SUPERVISORY BODIES [GOV-1]
heading: THE ROLE OF THE ADMIN ISTRATIVE , MANAGEMENT AND SUPE RVISORY BODIES [GOV-1]
start_phrase: As of 31 December 2024, the Management Board of PKO Bank Polski S.A. consisted of seven executive members: six men and one woman.
summary:
- Governance structure and composition:
  - As of 31 December 2024, the Management Board had seven executives (6 men, 1 woman; 17% women at year-end, avg. 11% in 2024). The Supervisory Board had eight non-executive, all independent members (33% women at year-end, avg. 47% in 2024).
  - Clear internal division of Management Board responsibilities across strategy, audit, security, compliance/conduct/reputation risk, legal, HR, marketing/communications, retail/corporate banking, corporate & investment banking, finance/accounting/tax/sustainable development, administration, operations/international banking/remote channels, technology, and risk management (all risks except compliance/conduct/reputation; includes restructuring and recoveries).
  - Board members have senior banking/financial market experience; periodic individual and collective suitability assessments; appointment of the President and the risk-management Board member requires Polish FSA approval.
  - Supervisory Board members meet State Treasury company criteria and bring academic, business, and audit/banking oversight experience.
  - Diversity snapshot (31 Dec 2024): Supervisory Board 2 women/6 men; Management Board 1 woman/6 men; Material Risk Takers 18 women/66 men. Age: no members below 30; Supervisory Board mostly 50+; Management Board balanced between 30–50 and 50+; MRTs mostly 30–50.

- Sustainability governance and competencies:
  - ESG knowledge development guided by regulations, needs assessments, mandatory training reports, inspections, and role/qualification analyses.
  - ESG knowledge and the ability to manage ESG risk are verification criteria in preliminary and annual suitability assessments (individual and collective) for the Management and Supervisory Boards.
  - Performance reviews include monitoring non-financial indicators and ESG goals, management objectives tied to strategy, and organizational impacts on stakeholders and society.
  - 2024 workshops for the Sustainable Development Committee (SDC), Management Board, and Supervisory Board covered climate competitiveness, carbon footprints, supply-chain mechanisms, financial institution requirements, climate strategy integration, Poland’s energy mix, evolving standards (SBTi, CDP, TCFD), and footprint reduction methods.

- Sustainable Development Committee (SDC):
  - Primary advisory body to the Management Board on significant impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs); oversees sustainability and energy transition initiatives; supports priority-setting, action plans, goals, and the sustainability management framework.
  - Meets at least quarterly; chaired by the VP for Finance and Accounting with the VP for Risk as deputy; two Management Board members participate, and the Board reviews minutes and reports.
  - Subordinate to the Management Board, which may amend its mandate; coordinates with other committees; exclusions include matters under the Credit Committee (e.g., limits and credit policies).
  - Recommends objectives, action plans, and timelines based on IRO analyses; monitors progress, accepts reports, and issues recommendations to the Management Board (and, when needed, the Supervisory Board).

- Information to governing bodies (GOV-2):
  - 2024: first ESRS-aligned double materiality analysis completed; future analyses to be performed when new IRO indicators emerge.
  - Management Board approved the list of significant IROs, integrated into strategy oversight via the SDC and Strategy Committee.
  - Key IROs overseen by SDC:
    - Impacts: client-portfolio GHG emissions; financing high-CO2 sectors; green fleet financing; reduced energy dependence; improved competitiveness.
    - Risks: rising investment needs in sustainable energy/efficiency; new building energy regulations; volatility in carbon allowance prices.
    - Opportunities: energy storage, energy infrastructure investment, CO2-limiting regulations, demand for CO2-reduction financing, green bonds growth, low-emission transport, renewables in construction, sustainable energy demand, EV charging infrastructure.

- Incentives and remuneration integration (GOV-3):
  - Remuneration policies for Supervisory and Management Boards and Material Risk Takers align with social interest, environmental protection, and mitigation of negative social impacts, and link to strategy execution.
  - Variable pay for Management Board members is tied to achieving ESG goals embedded in the Bank’s Strategy via KPIs for strategic initiatives; KPI outcomes affect performance bonuses.
text:
As of 31 December 2024, the Management Board of PKO  Bank Polski S.A. consisted of seven executive members: six 
men and one woman. The proportion of women on the Management Board at the end of the year was 17%, with an 
average of 11% throughout the year.  
As at the end of 2024, the internal division of responsibilities within the Bank's Management Board is as follows:  
• The President of the Management Board is specifically responsible for matters related to strategy, internal audit, 
security, compliance risk , conduct risk, reputational risk, legal services, human resources management, 
communication and marketing, as well as corporate governance oversight;  
• The Vice -President of the Management Board in charge of the Retail and Corporate Banking area is responsi ble 
in particular for matters relating to the development of the product offering for private individuals, including the 
design of the investment banking and insurance offering, product sales and services to private individuals and 
companies;  
• The Vice -President of the Management Board in charge of the Corporate and Investment Banking Division is 
responsible in particular for matters relating to investment banking, the provision of custody services, the 
development of the Bank's treasury product offering and  its own activities in the financial market, the development 
of the product offering for companies, enterprises and corporate and public sector banking customers, the sale 
of products to these customers, excluding companies;  
• The Vice -President of the Manag ement Board in charge of the Finance and Accounting Division is responsible in 
particular for the following matters: macroeconomic analysis, financial planning and controlling, accounting and 
financial reporting, taxation and sustainable development;   
• The Vice-President of the Management Board in charge of the Administration Division is responsible in particular 
for the Bank's property management and procurement matters;  
• The Vice -President of the Management Board in charge of the Operations and Internationa l Banking Division is 
responsible, in particular, for the handling of operations, the customer advocacy function, the sale of products 
and the servicing of international and institutional banking customers, the servicing of customers via means of 
remote co mmunication, product administration and cash management;  
• The Vice -President of the Management Board in charge of the Technology Division is responsible in particular 
for IT matters;  
• The Vice -President of the Management Board in charge of the Risk Managemen t Division is responsible in 
particular for the management of all risks relating to the Bank's activities, excluding compliance risk, conduct risk 
and reputation risk, as well as matters relating to the restructuring and recovery of the Bank's receivables.   
All members of the Bank's Management Board have extensive experience in banking and financial market institutions 
at the highest executive levels. They also possess knowledge and expertise relevant to the specific areas under their 
supervision (e.g. bankin g risk, information technology, financial reporting).  
The competencies and experience of the Management Board members are periodically assessed as part of both 
individual and collective suitability evaluations of the governing body as a whole. Additionall y, in accordance with 
Polish banking supervisory requirements, the appointment of the President of the Management Board and the 
Management Board member responsible for risk management requires the approval of the Polish Financial 
Supervision Authority, whi ch takes into account, among other factors, the candidate’s experience when making its 
decision.  
As of 31 December 2024, the Supervisory Board consisted of eight non -executive  members, all of whom were 
designated as independent members.  The proportion of women on the Supervisory Board at the end of the year was 
33%, with an average of 4 7% throughout the year.  
In accordance with formal requirements, all members of the Supervisory Board meet the specified qualification criteria 
required for members of the s upervisory bodies of companies with State Treasury participation. The members of the 
Supervisory Board of PKO Bank Polski S.A. represent academic, business, and audit -advisory circles. They have 
documented extensive experience in academic work at higher ed ucation institutions, serving on the supervisory 
boards of financial sector companies, and holding senior management positions in banking and audit.  THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP  
DIRECTOR’S REPORT FOR 2024

At the Bank, matters related to enhancing the necessary expertise in sustainable development are determined based 
on internal and external regulations, needs assessments —including those aligned with planned activities, particularly 
in the context of strate gic objectives — reports on mandatory ESG training, post -inspection recommendations, as well 
as an analysis of employee qualifications, roles, and responsibilities.   
Assessment of the knowledge, skills and experience of members of the Management Board and Supervisory Board 
of the Bank on sustainable development, including the ability to manage ESG risk and the impact of ESG risk factors 
on Bank's operations, is one of the verification criteria as part of preliminary and periodic (annual) suitability 
assessments and collective suitability assessments. Performance review of the Bank's Management Board and 
Supervisory Board with regard to fulfilment of entrusted obligation s, including monitoring the management of the 
organisation's impact on ESG issues, is assessed in several respects, including through periodic monitoring of: the 
achievement of non -financial indicators and ESG -related objectives, the management objectives of the Bank’s 
Management Board members — including the implementation of the Bank’s strategy — as well as the organisation’s 
impact on stakeholders and the social environment.  
In 2024, as part of skills development and knowledge enhancement, the Bank impl emented, among other initiatives:  
• a strategic workshop for members of the Sustainable Development Committee, as well as other members of the 
Management Board and Supervisory Board of the Bank, focusing on corporate climate competitiveness and the 
role of f inancial institutions;  
• a workshop on an in -depth understanding of carbon footprint and corporate climate competitiveness for 
members of the Management Board and Supervisory Board of the Bank.  
Both workshops addressed the broader context of climate change a nd the role of businesses in its mitigation, the 
impact of climate change on business, supply chain -related mechanisms and financial institutions' requirements, 
climate strategy as an element of business strategy and a tool for building competitive advanta ge, the position of 
companies in the context of Poland's energy mix and the relative progress of climate initiatives, the evolution of 
corporate carbon footprint reporting standards (SBTi, CDP, TCFD), and methods for reducing carbon footprint across 
differ ent areas and asset classes.  
The Sustainable Development Committee of PKO Bank Polski S.A. is responsible for overseeing the impacts, risks, and 
opportunities of the Bank’s Group. This responsibility is reflected in the objectives and competencies assigne d to the 
Committee through a formal resolution. The Committee serves as the primary advisory body to the Management 
Board, responsible for monitoring, managing, and supervising impacts, risks, and opportunities related to the Bank’s 
Group. The Committee's objectives include overseeing the implementation of the Bank’s and the Bank’s Group’s 
sustainability and energy transition initiatives, supporting the Management Board in setting priorities, action plans, 
and sustainability goals, and shaping the sustainab le development management framework. As part of its monitoring, 
management, and supervisory procedures, the Committee is required to hold meetings as needed, but no less than 
once per quarter. Within its competencies, the Management Board makes decisions o n the Bank’s sustainability 
matters, particularly based on recommendations from the Sustainable Development Committee. The Management 
Board oversees the Committee through the participation of two Management Board members in its activities and by 
reviewing meeting minutes and reports on its operations. The Committee is chaired by the Vice President of the 
Management Board responsible for finance and accounting, with the Vice President responsible for risk oversight 
serving as the deputy.  
The Sustainable Development Committee is subordinate to the Management Board, which is specifically authorized 
to amend the Committee's objectives, competencies, and composition. It is also empowered to make decisions that 
serve as the basis for actions by  the Bank's bodies and committees, as well as to collaborate with other committees 
within the Bank. The Committee's competencies take into account the distinct roles and responsibilities of other THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP

specific matters from the Committee's competencies are outlined in the relevant internal regulations. The regulations 
establishing the Sustainable Development Committee exclude matters within the compe tence of the Bank's Credit 
Committee, particularly concerning limits and credit policies, from the scope of the Sustainable Development 
Committee's recommendations regarding the application of ESG indicators in the Bank's operations, including in the

title: INFORMATION PROVIDED TO ADMINISTRATIVE, MANAGEMENT AND SUPERVISORY BODIES [GOV-2]
heading: INFORMATION PROVIDED TO ADMINISTRATIVE , MANAGEMENT AND SUPE RVISORY BODIES [GOV-2]
start_phrase: In 2024, the Bank conducted its first double materiality analysis in accordance with the European Sust ainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) and due diligence principles.
summary:
- Outlines the role of the Sustainable Development Committee (SDC) in PKO Bank Polski’s governance, including supporting the Management Board in setting ESG priorities, action plans, goals, and timelines, and monitoring progress through required reports and recommendations.
- Clarifies competency boundaries: SDC excludes matters under the Bank’s Credit Committee (e.g., credit limits and policies) when applying ESG indicators to products and services.
- Describes information flows to administrative, management, and supervisory bodies, noting the Bank’s first double materiality analysis conducted in 2024 under ESRS and due diligence principles, with future analyses triggered by new indicators of significant impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs).
- States that the Management Board approved the list of significant IROs, with oversight performed by the SDC and the Strategy Committee.
- Summarizes key IROs:
  - Impacts: client portfolio greenhouse gas emissions, financing high-CO2 companies, green fleet financing, reduced energy dependence, improved competitiveness.
  - Risks: higher investment needs in sustainable energy/efficiency, new building energy consumption regulations, sudden rises in carbon allowance prices.
  - Opportunities: energy storage, energy infrastructure investment, tighter CO2 regulations, demand for CO2-reduction financial services, growth of green bonds, low-emission public transport and economy, renewable energy in construction, rising demand for sustainable energy, EV charging infrastructure development.
- Notes governance practice whereby, due to Management Board representation on the SDC, most decisions are taken at Committee level; only exceptional matters (e.g., acceptance of double materiality results) are escalated to the Management Board and Supervisory Board.
- Explains integration of sustainability into incentive schemes: remuneration policies require Management Board goals to reflect social interest, environmental protection, and mitigation of negative social impacts, aligned with Bank and Group strategy.
- Confirms variable remuneration for Management Board members is linked to ESG objectives embedded in strategic initiative KPIs, with KPI performance influencing bonuses.
text:
In 2024, the Bank conducted its first double materiality analysis in accordance with the European Sust ainability 
Reporting Standards (ESRS) and due diligence principles. Future analyses will be carried out periodically when there 
are indicators of new significant impacts, risks, and opportunities (IRO) . 
The list of significant impacts, risks, and opportuni ties was approved by the Management Board of PKO Bank Polski 
S.A. These are taken into account in the oversight of strategy implementation, within the Sustainable Development 
Committee and the Strategy Committee. Key IROs overseen by the Sustainable Develo pment Committee (KZR) 
include:  
• Impacts: Greenhouse gas emissions from the Bank's client portfolio, financing projects in companies with high 
CO 2 emissions, green financing for vehicle fleet leasing/modernization, potential reduction of dependence on 
energ y resources, improvement of economic competitiveness;  
• Risks: Increased demand for investments in sustainable energy and energy efficiency improvements, introduction 
of new regulations on required energy consumption levels for buildings, sudden increase in the price of carbon 
emission allowances;  
• Opportunities: Development of energy storage technologies, increased investment in energy infrastructure, 
introduction of new regulations limiting CO2 emissions, increased demand for financial services related to CO 2 
reduction projects, growth of the green bond market, increased investment in low -emission public transport 
infrastructure, growing importance of a low -emission economy, increased importance of renewable energy 
investments in construction, increased deman d for sustainable energy, development of electric vehicle charging 
infrastructure.  
Due to the presence of two members of the Management Board in the Sustainable Development Committee, most 
decisions are made by the Committee, and only in exceptional cases does the Committee pass recommendations to 
the Management Board and Supervisory Board (e.g. acceptance of the double materiality analysis results).

title: INTEGRATION OF SUSTAINABILITY-RELATED PERFORMANCE IN INCENTIVE SCHEMES [GOV-3]
heading: INTEGRATION OF SUSTAI NABILITY -RELATED PERFORMANCE IN INCENTIVE SCHEMES [GOV-3]
start_phrase: The incentive schemes and remuneration principles for members of the governing, management, and supervisory bodies are based on the "Remuneration Policy for Members of the Supervisory Board and Management Board of Powszechna Kasa Oszczędności Banku Polskie go S.A." and the "Principles of Remuneration for Employees Whose Activities Have a Significant Impact on the Bank's Risk Profile."
summary:
- Governance framework: The Sustainable Development Committee supports the Management Board in setting sustainability priorities, action plans, goals, and implementation timelines. Its remit excludes matters reserved for the Credit Committee (e.g., limits and credit policies). It reviews progress, accepts reports/statements, and can issue recommendations; with two Management Board members on the Committee, most decisions are taken at Committee level, with only exceptional escalations (e.g., approval of double materiality results) to the Management Board/Supervisory Board.
- Information to governing bodies and double materiality: In 2024 the Bank conducted its first ESRS-aligned double materiality analysis following due diligence principles. Significant impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) were approved by the Management Board and are overseen within the Sustainable Development and Strategy Committees. Future analyses will be refreshed when new IRO indicators arise.
- Key IROs overseen:
  - Impacts: Client portfolio GHG emissions; financing to high-CO2 companies; green financing for fleet modernization; potential energy dependence reduction; competitiveness improvements.
  - Risks: Rising investment needs in sustainable energy/efficiency; new building energy-consumption regulations; sharp increases in carbon allowance prices.
  - Opportunities: Energy storage development; energy infrastructure investments; tighter CO2 regulations; growing demand for CO2-reduction finance; expansion of the green bond market; low-emission public transport; low-emission economy emphasis; renewable energy in construction; sustainable energy demand; EV charging infrastructure.
- Integration of sustainability into remuneration (incentives):
  - Management Board: Variable pay tied to achieving ESG-related strategic KPIs; goals must reflect social interest, environmental protection, and minimizing negative social impacts; decarbonization goals embedded in two strategic programs; in 2024, a diversity KPI (share of women in roles with significant risk impact) accounted for 10% as a corrective indicator. Exact climate-linked pay share cannot be isolated.
  - Supervisory Board: Fixed remuneration only; assesses Management Board effectiveness on ESG via performance approvals.
  - Group companies: No direct pay link for boards/supervisory boards, but management goals should align with Group ESG targets for 2025–2027.
  - Material Risk Takers (including Management Board): MbO-based goals with risk-sensitive criteria; bonuses adjustable per the Annual Note, with upward adjustments capped at 100% of fixed pay. Payouts for Management Board contingent on General Meeting approval of financials, discharge, and compliance with public/state property management requirements (incl. “chimney act”). Variable pay may be reduced for misconduct, legal/standard breaches, poor task performance, or inappropriate behavior.
  - Approval of schemes: Management Board remuneration frameworks approved by the General Meeting and Supervisory Board; MRT principles approved by the Bank’s Management Board.
- Employee representation: Employees are represented by trade unions, the Bank Employee Council, and Social Labour Inspection; the Bank does not impede participation and cooperates per applicable regulations.
- Due diligence statement: The Group applies ongoing, proactive due diligence to identify, prevent, and mitigate negative impacts; process elements are detailed throughout the report.
text:
The incentive schemes and remuneration principles for members of the governing, management, and supervisory 
bodies are based on the "Remuneration Policy for Members of the Supervisory Board and Management Board of 
Powszechna Kasa Oszczędności Banku Polskie go S.A." and the "Principles of Remuneration for Employees Whose 
Activities Have a Significant Impact on the Bank's Risk Profile."   
The Remuneration Policy for members of the Supervisory Board and Management Board of Powszechna Kasa 
Oszczędności Banku Pol skiego S.A. stipulates that the management goals of individual members of the Management 
Board should, in accordance with their area of responsibility, take into account criteria such as ensuring the Bank's 
commitment to considering the social interest and  contributing to environmental protection and preventing or 
mitigating any negative social impacts of the Bank's activities. Additionally, the management goals should relate to 
the implementation of the Bank's and the Bank’s Group's strategy. Given the abo ve, the variable remuneration of the 
Bank's Management Board members is linked to the achievement of ESG goals set out in the Bank's Strategy. This 
means that the ESG goals related to climate are addressed in the KPIs of individual strategic initiatives. T he evaluation 
of these KPIs influences the achievement of strategic goals reflected in the Management Board's performance 
bonuses.  THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP  
DIRECTOR’S REPORT FOR 2024  
prepared jointly with the PKO Bank Polski S.A Director’s Report   
 
 Strona 173/288 
 
 
 Members of the Supervisory Board are entitled solely to fixed remuneration. Within their competence and role in the 
governanc e of sustainability issues, they assess the effectiveness of the Management Board in achieving ESG goals 
by approving the Management Board's performance review for the relevant period, which also indirectly relates to 
their role in the climate governance s ystem.  
The remuneration policy for employees of the Bank and the Bank’s Group does not directly link the remuneration of 
members of the boards and supervisory boards of companies within the Bank's Group to sustainability issues. 
However, their management goals should, as a rule, be consistent across the entire Bank’s Group and ensure support 
for the achievement of the ESG goals outlined in the Bank's Strategy for 2025 -2027.  
In 2024, the evaluation of the Management Board's performance was dependent, among  other factors, on the 
achievement of a sustainability -related goal, which concerned the percentage of women holding positions with a 
significant impact on the Bank's risk profile. This goal accounts for 10% of the Bank's score, which is a corrective 
indicator for the variable remuneration amount. However, the performance notes for the members of the Management 
Board included a goal related to assessing progress towards achieving the long -term assumptions and objectives of 
the strategic programmes resulting  from the strategy adopted by the Bank. Goals related to decarbonisation are 
present in two strategic programmes. It is not possible to isolate the percentage of remuneration dependent on 
climate -related goals.  
The basis for granting variable components o f remuneration for MRT (employees whose activities have a significant 
impact on the Bank's risk profile), including members of the Management Board, is primarily the performance goals 
set within the framework of management by objectives (MbO). The MbO goal s ensure consideration of the Bank’s 
economic cycle and the risks associated with its activities. The risk is taken into account by setting appropriate, risk -
sensitive criteria for evaluating the performance of MRTs.  
The amount of the bonus for each MRT f or the given performance period, including members of the Management 
Board of the Bank and its subsidiaries, may be adjusted depending on the degree of achievement of the goals defined 
in the so -called Annual Note of the Bank, but not exceeding 100% of the  fixed remuneration in the case of an upward 
adjustment.  
For members of the Management Board, the condition for awarding and initiating bonus payments is the approval 
by the General Meeting of the financial statement for the relevant performance period, gr anting discharge to the 
Board members, and achieving management goals related to the obligation to implement the requirements of public 
regulations regarding state property management and the so -called "chimney act."  
Any of the calculated variable remuner ation components may be reduced as a result of: violation of employee duties, 
failure to comply with legal provisions or customer service standards, improper performance of assigned tasks, or 
behaviour towards other employees that violates social cohabitat ion principles.  
The conditions of the incentive schemes are approved and updated at the Bank:  
• for the Management Board, at the General Meeting within the framework of the Remuneration Policy for Members 
of the Supervisory Board and Management Board and at  the level of the Supervisory Board adopting the 
Principles of Employment and Remuneration for Members of the Management Board of the Bank;  
• for employees of the Bank, at the level of the Management Board, which adopts the Principles of Remuneration 
for Emp loyees Whose Activities Have a Significant Impact on the Bank's Risk Profile – Material Risk Takers in the 
Bank.

title: EMPLOYEE REPRESENTATION [GOV-1]
heading: EMPLOYEE REPRESENTATI ON [GOV-1]
start_phrase: Employees are represented at the Bank by the trade unions, the Bank Employee Council and the Social Labour Inspection.
summary:
- Supervisory Board members receive only fixed remuneration and oversee sustainability governance by assessing the Management Board’s effectiveness through approval of performance reviews, linking indirectly to climate governance.
- Remuneration policy does not directly tie board and supervisory board pay to sustainability metrics, but management goals are aligned with the Bank’s 2025–2027 ESG Strategy.
- In 2024, Management Board evaluation included a sustainability metric on the share of women in roles significantly affecting the Bank’s risk profile; this accounts for 10% of the Bank’s score used to adjust variable remuneration.
- Decarbonisation objectives are embedded in two strategic programmes, though the portion of remuneration tied specifically to climate goals cannot be isolated.
- Variable pay for Material Risk Takers (MRTs), including Management Board members, is based on management by objectives (MbO) with risk-sensitive criteria reflecting the economic cycle and risk profile.
- Bonuses for MRTs may be adjusted based on the Bank’s Annual Note, with upward adjustments capped at 100% of fixed remuneration.
- Payment of Management Board bonuses requires General Meeting approval of financial statements, discharge of Board members, and achievement of management goals, including compliance with public regulations on state property management and the “chimney act.”
- Variable remuneration can be reduced for violations of duties, legal non-compliance, poor task performance, customer service breaches, or behavior infringing social cohabitation principles.
- Incentive scheme governance: for the Management Board, policies are set by the General Meeting and Supervisory Board; for MRT employees, principles are set by the Management Board.
- Employee representation is ensured via trade unions, the Bank Employee Council, and Social Labour Inspection, with the employer supporting participation and cooperation per regulations.
- Due diligence is applied as a continuous, proactive process to identify, prevent, or mitigate negative impacts, with detailed elements described elsewhere in the report.
text:
Employees are represented at the Bank by the trade unions, the Bank Employee Council and the Social Labour 
Inspection. The employer does not prevent the employees from joining the trade unions and the Bank Employee 
Council or acting as their members in any way. The Bank cooperates with these social partners in accordance with 
the applicable regulations. For a deta iled description of the cooperation on employee representation, see section 
13.3.1 “Own workforce”.

title: STATEMENT ON DUE DILIGENCE [GOV-4]
heading: STATEMENT ON DUE DILI GENCE [GOV-4]
start_phrase: The Bank’s Group applies the principle of due diligence through a continuous and proactive process aimed at identifying negative impacts and making decisions to exclude or reduce them.
summary:
- Governance and remuneration in relation to sustainability:
  - Supervisory Board members receive fixed remuneration only; they assess Management Board effectiveness on ESG by approving performance reviews, indirectly contributing to climate governance.
  - Group remuneration policies do not directly tie board pay to sustainability; however, management goals across the Group are expected to support ESG objectives in the 2025–2027 Strategy.
  - In 2024, Management Board evaluation included a sustainability metric: the share of women in roles significantly affecting the Bank’s risk profile (10% weighting as a corrective indicator for variable pay).
  - Strategic programme goals, including decarbonisation in two programmes, inform performance notes; the climate-linked share of remuneration cannot be isolated.
  - Variable pay for Material Risk Takers (MRTs), including Management Board members, is set via Management by Objectives with risk-sensitive criteria; potential upward adjustment capped at 100% of fixed pay and contingent on GM approval of financials, discharge, and compliance with state property and “chimney act” requirements.
  - Variable components may be reduced for misconduct, legal non-compliance, poor task performance, or inappropriate behavior.
  - Incentive scheme governance: GM and Supervisory Board approve policies for Management Board; Management Board approves MRT remuneration principles for employees.

- Employee representation:
  - Employees are represented by trade unions, the Bank Employee Council, and Social Labour Inspection; the Bank does not restrict participation and cooperates per regulations, with further detail referenced in the workforce section.

- Due diligence statement:
  - The Group applies a continuous, proactive due diligence process to identify, prevent, and mitigate negative impacts.
  - Core elements of due diligence (governance embedding, stakeholder engagement, impact identification, mitigation actions, and effectiveness tracking) are mapped to dedicated chapters/ESRS references in the report.

- Risk management and internal controls:
  - An internal control system supports effective operations, reliable reporting, risk management compliance, and legal/regulatory adherence, including the reporting process.
  - Key non-compliance risks in external reporting (deadlines, data quality, classification, missing disclosures) are mitigated via partial automation, verification, audits, controls, and authorizations; overall risk assessed as moderate.
  - Work is in progress to incorporate sustainability reporting risk into the reporting process.
  - No dedicated integration of sustainability-reporting control findings into internal functions yet; 2025 internal audit plan excludes sustainability reporting, with potential inclusion in the 2026–2028 strategic plan based on risk assessment.
  - Internal audit results are reported to the Management Board, Audit Committee, Supervisory Board, and the PFSA Office (for the Bank and Bank Hipoteczny).

- Double materiality assessment (2024):
  - First ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment conducted with external experts at Group and subsidiary levels, covering own activities and exposures (asset structure, sectoral credit exposure, geographic distribution).
  - Broad stakeholder engagement via a survey (targeted 330,483 stakeholders) from 13 Aug to 20 Sep 2024, including subsidiaries, employees, external stakeholders, and experts.
  - Comprehensive scoping produced initial lists of 245 impacts, 165 risks, and 119 opportunities, developed with input from experts across key Bank and subsidiary departments.

title: RISK MANAGEMENT AND INTERNAL CONTROLS [GOV-5]
heading: RISK MANAGEMENT AND I NTERNAL CONTROLS [GOV-5]
start_phrase: The Bank Group has an internal control system that is adapted to the type and scale of its business.
summary:
- Outlines the core due diligence elements in the Sustainability Statement, including governance/strategy integration, stakeholder engagement, identification and assessment of adverse impacts, actions to address them, and tracking/communication, with references to relevant ESRS disclosures.
- Describes the Group’s internal control system tailored to its business scale, ensuring operational effectiveness, reliable reporting, and compliance with laws, internal regulations, supervisory recommendations, and market standards.
- Details the external reporting process and key non-compliance risks (missed statutory deadlines, data quality issues, misclassification, missing disclosures), along with mitigation measures such as partial automation, ongoing verification, audits, controls, and report authorization; overall risk assessed as moderate.
- Notes ongoing work to incorporate sustainability reporting risks into the reporting-control framework; currently no dedicated integration of sustainability reporting control findings into internal functions.
- States that the 2025 internal audit plan excludes a sustainability reporting audit; potential inclusion in the 2026–2028 strategic audit plan will depend on future analysis and risk assessment. Audit results are regularly submitted to governing bodies and, for the Bank and Bank Hipoteczny, to the PFSA Office.
- Presents the Group’s first double materiality assessment (2024), aligned with ESRS, conducted at Group and subsidiary levels, covering own activities, asset structure, sectoral credit exposures, and geographic portfolio distribution, supported by external experts.
- Explains stakeholder engagement via a large-scale survey (Aug 13–Sep 20, 2024) targeting 330,483 stakeholders, including subsidiaries’ representatives, employees, external stakeholders, and experts, to validate key impact and financial materiality topics.
- Reports the development of an initial universe of 245 impacts, 165 risks, and 119 opportunities, assessed by experts from key Bank departments and subsidiaries with external support, leading into impact materiality analysis.
text:
The Bank Group has an internal control system that is adapted to the type and scale of its business. The internal 
control system supports the management of the Bank and the Bank's Group Companies by ensuring the effectiveness 
and efficiency of operations, the reliability of reporting, compliance with the risk management principles and 
compliance of operations with generally applicable laws, the internal regulations, supervisory recommendations and 
market standards. The internal control system covers, among other things, the process of preparing reports to ensure 
effective and reliable operations, reliability of disclosures presented and compliance with laws, internal regulations 
and best market practices and standards.   
The Bank has established a process for the external reporting of the Bank and the Bank's Group. As part of the 
identification and assessment of non -compliance risks for this process, particular attention is given to the potential 
risks associated with exce eding statutory deadlines for the preparation and submission of reports, improper 
preparation of reports due to the quality of data in source systems, incorrect classification of information, and 
omission of required disclosures. The risk is mitigated, amo ng other things, through partial automation of the process, 
ongoing verification, audits, controls, and authorisation of reports. The overall risk level has been assessed as 
moderate. Work is underway to include the risk of sustainability reporting within the framework of this process.    
The Bank's Group has not implemented methods for integrating findings from internal controls dedicated to 
sustainability reporting into its internal functions and processes. The internal audit plan for 2025 does not includ e an 
audit on sustainability reporting. A strategic internal audit plan for 2026 -2028 will be developed in 2025. The inclusion 
of an audit on the preparation of sustainability reporting by the Bank will depend on the results of the conducted 
analysis and r isk assessment. The results of internal audits conducted at the Bank and its Subsidiaries are periodically 
submitted to the supervisory bodies (the Management Board, the Audit Committee of the Supervisory Board, and the 
Supervisory Board), and additionally , for the Bank and Bank Hipoteczny, they are submitted to the PFSA Office.

title: DOUBLE MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY AND PROCESS
heading: DOUBLE MATERIALITY AS SESSMENT METHODOLOGY AND PROCESS
start_phrase: In 2024, the Bank's Group conducted its first double materiality assessment aime d at identifying key issues related to impacts, risks, and opportunities related to sustainable development.
summary:
- Outlines the core elements of the Sustainability Statement’s due diligence chapter, aligned with ESRS references: embedding due diligence in governance/strategy/business model; engaging affected stakeholders; identifying and assessing adverse impacts; taking action to address them; and tracking effectiveness and communicating.
- Describes the Group’s internal control system and risk management for reporting: ensures operational effectiveness, reliable disclosures, and legal/regulatory compliance; identifies key non-compliance risks in external reporting (deadlines, data quality, misclassification, missing disclosures) and mitigation measures (partial automation, verification, audits, controls, authorizations). Overall reporting risk assessed as moderate.
- Notes ongoing work to incorporate sustainability reporting risk into reporting processes; no dedicated integration of sustainability reporting control findings yet; 2025 internal audit plan excludes sustainability reporting, with potential inclusion in the 2026–2028 plan based on risk assessment. Audit results are reported to governing bodies and, for the Bank and Bank Hipoteczny, to the PFSA.
- Presents the Group’s first double materiality assessment (2024), compliant with ESRS and supported by external experts, covering Group and subsidiaries, own activities and exposures (asset structure, sector credit exposure, geographic distribution).
- Details stakeholder engagement via a large survey (13 Aug–20 Sep 2024) sent to 330,483 stakeholders (subsidiary reps, employees, external stakeholders, experts) to validate key topics.
- Builds an initial universe of 245 impacts, 165 risks, and 119 opportunities; evaluations conducted by cross-functional internal experts with external support.
- Explains impact materiality methodology: assesses actual/potential, positive/negative impacts using scale, scope, reversibility (severity), and likelihood on a five-point scale; expert-defined thresholds determine materiality.
- Explains financial materiality for risks/opportunities: assessed by likelihood and potential financial consequences (using Group gross profit and gross carrying value); ESG risk treated as cross-cutting and not yet integrated into overall risk management; opportunity management tied to strategic objectives; uses historical data, forecasts, and expert judgment; high/very high ratings deemed material.
- Reports outcomes: selection of key issues across five topics (climate change, own employee resources, consumers and end-users, business conduct, and others); approvals on 24 Oct, 18 Nov, and 27 Nov 2024; results underpin sustainability disclosures (Tables 36–39).
- Summarizes environmental materiality results (Table 36): climate change mitigation and energy are material for impacts/risks/opportunities; climate change adaptation is material for impacts and opportunities (not risks); pollution (air/water/soil, substances, microplastics), water and marine resources, biodiversity and ecosystems, and circular economy topics are not material.
text:
In 2024, the Bank's Group conducted its first double materiality assessment aime d at identifying key issues related 
to impacts, risks, and opportunities related to sustainable development. The assessment was performed in line with 
the guidelines of the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), with support from external cons ultancy 
experts. The materiality assessment was carried out both at the Group level and for each subsidiary . The analysis 
covered the Bank's own activities and exposures, including the structure of the Group's assets, with particular focus 
on banking asset s, credit exposure across economic sectors, and the geographical distribution of the portfolio.  
To ensure the comprehensiveness of the double materiality assessment, stakeholders were engaged through a survey 
designed to validate the key topics from the p erspective of the Group's impact and the influence of the environment 
on the Group. The survey was directed to selected stakeholder groups, including representatives from subsidiaries, 
employees of the Bank’s Group, external stakeholders, and experts. The survey ran from 13 August to 20 September 
2024 and targeted 330,483 stakeholders . 
The materiality assessment began with the development of a list of 245 impacts, 165 risks, and 119 opportunities 
facing the Bank’s Group in the context of identified sustaina ble development issues. The process of creating the list 
and assessing individual impacts, risks, and opportunities involved a wide range of experts from key departments 
within the Bank and its subsidiaries, supported by external experts.

title: IMPACT MATERIALITY
heading: IMPACT MATERIALI TY
start_phrase: The process of double materiality assessment began with the creation of a list of impacts resulting from both the Bank's own activities and its value chain, which were evaluated using a dedicated tool to determine their actual, potential, positive, or negative nature .
summary:
- Focus: Description of PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 double materiality assessment methodology, governance, and outcomes, forming the basis for sustainability disclosures.
- Impact materiality: Identified impacts across own operations and value chain; assessed on a five-point scale using four parameters—scale, scope, reversibility (defining severity), and likelihood. Impacts above an expert-set cut-off were deemed material.
- Financial materiality: Assessed via likelihood and potential financial consequences, referencing the Group’s gross profit and gross carrying value; aligned post hoc with impact results; five-point scale applied.
- Risk/opportunity assessment: Tools for risks and opportunities slightly differ; ESG risk treated as cross-cutting (not a standalone risk type). The identification, evaluation, and management of IRO are not yet integrated into the Bank’s overall risk management process.
- Opportunities: Identified, evaluated, and managed primarily through the operationalization of strategic objectives.
- Evidence base: Historical data, market forecasts, and expert analyses underpin evaluations. Risks/opportunities rated high or very high were considered material.
- Outcome: 15 material issues identified (13 in impacts/opportunities and 6 in risks), grouped into five topics: climate change, own employee resources, consumers and end-users, business conduct, and others.
- Approvals and governance: Results validated internally (24 Oct 2024), by the Sustainable Development Committee (18 Nov 2024), and the Management Board (27 Nov 2024).
- Disclosure linkage: Results underpin Group sustainability disclosures (Tables 36–37), the list of ESRS disclosure requirements (Table 38), and other EU data points (Table 39).
- Table 36 highlights (Environment):
  - Material: Climate change mitigation (E1) — impacts, risks, opportunities; Climate change adaptation (E1) — impacts and opportunities (not risk); Energy (E1) — impacts, risks, opportunities.
  - Not material: Pollution (E2) across all subtopics; Water and marine resources (E3); Biodiversity and ecosystems (E4); Circular economy (E5).
text:
The process of double materiality assessment began with the creation of a list of impacts resulting from both the 
Bank's own activities and its value chain, which were evaluated using a dedicated tool to determine their actual, 
potential, positive, or negative nature . The basis for assessing the materiality of impacts was four parameters: scale, 
scope, reversibility, which contributed to the severity of the impact, as well as the likelihood of occurrence . Each of 
these parameters was assessed using a fi ve-point scale (very low, low, medium, high, very high). The selection and 
prioritisation of topics in the area of impacts were based on expert -established materiality thresholds. Any impact 
whose score exceeded the established cut -off point was considered  material .

title: FINANCIAL MATERIALITY
heading: FINANCIAL MATERIALITY
start_phrase: Due to the schedule of the double materiality assessment process, the evaluation of risks and opportunities began before the impact materiality assessment was completed.
summary:
- Scope and purpose: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 double materiality assessment under ESRS to identify material impacts, risks, and opportunities across own operations and the value chain, informing sustainability disclosures.
- Methodology for impact materiality: identification of actual/potential, positive/negative impacts; assessment parameters include scale, scope, reversibility, and likelihood; five-point rating; expert-defined thresholds determine materiality.
- Financial materiality approach: assessed via likelihood and potential financial consequences relative to Group gross profit and gross carrying value; five-point scales; based on historical data, forecasts, and expert judgment; items rated high/very high deemed material.
- Risk and opportunity governance: ESG risk treated as cross-cutting (not standalone); IRO identification/evaluation/management not yet integrated into the overall risk framework; opportunities managed through strategic objective operationalization.
- Validation and disclosure: results endorsed internally (24 Oct 2024), by the Sustainable Development Committee (18 Nov 2024), and Management Board (27 Nov 2024); underpin sustainability report disclosures and data mapping to EU requirements (Tables 36–39).
- Material topics selected: 15 issues mapped to five themes—climate change, own workforce, consumers and end-users, business conduct, and “other” (e.g., infrastructure, state security). Environmental subtopics on pollution, water/marine resources, biodiversity, and circular economy were not deemed material.
- Climate change (E1): mitigation, adaptation, and energy are material (impacts/opportunities; risks material for mitigation and energy but not for adaptation). Key impact areas include financed emissions, financing in high-CO2 sectors and disaster-prone areas, and support for transition/adaptation. Risks span transition dynamics (carbon pricing/taxes, regulatory shifts, supply chain constraints, social acceptance) and governance gaps at clients. Opportunities include energy storage, green bonds, growing demand for emission-reduction finance, low-emission transport and charging infrastructure, energy-efficient real estate, and low-emission construction.
- Own workforce (S1): material impacts/opportunities in working conditions and equal treatment (health, safety, ergonomics, development, anti-harassment, data security); opportunities in pay benchmarking, social dialogue, collective bargaining, work–life balance, and training.
- Consumers and end-users (S4): material impacts/opportunities in information quality, personal safety, inclusion, privacy/cybersecurity, fair communication/advice; opportunities in stronger security standards, non-discrimination, and financing safety/health-related innovation.
- Business conduct (G1): material across corporate culture, whistleblower protection, corruption/bribery, and political engagement (as a risk). Emphasis on reputation, compliance, preventing abuses, AML/CFT effectiveness, and culture resilience; opportunities from embedding sustainability and robust whistleblower frameworks.
- Other material issues: development of industry and strategic infrastructure (energy, defense, raw materials) and product compliance; opportunity-only item on operating amid/post conflict; risk of environmental degradation from financed industrial activities; opportunities in post-conflict reconstruction and infrastructure build-out, and product certification programs.
- Climate assessment process (E1.IRO-1): identified 6 material impacts, 10 risks, 11 opportunities; considered short-, medium-, and long-term horizons; combined qualitative/quantitative analysis using sector (NACE) exposure and emissions; financial impacts tied to exposed assets and gross profit. Findings highlight high exposure to portfolio emissions and transition risk, moderate adaptation risk, and significant growth potential in supporting sustainable energy, low-emission technologies, and early-stage energy storage in Poland.
text:
FINANCIAL MATERIALITY   
Due to the schedule of the double materiality assessment process, the evaluation of risks and opportunities began 
before the impact materiality assessment was completed. To meet the requirement for linking risks, opportuni ties, and 
impacts, a verification of the list of risks and opportunities was conducted after the impact assessment had concluded. 
The basis for financial materiality was two parameters: the likelihood of occurrence and potential financial 
consequences. The  analysis of financial consequences used the gross profit of the Group and its gross carrying value. 
Similar to the impact materiality assessment, each characteristic was rated on a five -point scale (very low, low, 
medium, high, very high) . 
The tools used to assess risks and opportunities showed a slight degree of differentiation. They reflected the fact that 
ESG risk is not a separate, but a cross -cutting type of risk, defined as the risk of negative financial effects for the 
Bank, resulting from the curre nt or future impact of ESG risk factors on customers, counterparties, or the Bank's 
balance sheet positions. The process of identification, evaluation, and management of IRO has not yet been integrated 
into the overall risk management process.  
In the case  of opportunities, the processes of identification, evaluation, and management are carried out solely in the 
context of operationalising strategic objectives.  
Evaluations of both risks and opportunities were based on historical data, market forecasts, and expert analysis. 
Based on the obtained individual evaluations, materiality thresholds were set, which formed the basis for selecting 
the most important issues. Risks or opportunities evaluated as high or very high were considered material.  
The result of t he double materiality assessment was the selection of a list of 15 issues (13 in the area of impacts and 
opportunities, and 6 in the area of risks), assigned to 5 topics: climate change, own employee resources, consumers 
and end -users, business conduct, an d others.   
The results were approved at an internal meeting (24 October  2024), and subsequently by the Sustainable 
Development Committee (18 November 2024) and the Management Board (27 November 2024). The results of the 
analysis form the basis for disclos ures for the Bank’s Group and are presented in Tables 36 and 37. The list of 
disclosure requirements met during the preparation of the sustainability report is in Table 38. Table 39. includes data 
points resulting from other EU regulations.

title: DESCRIPTION OF THE PROCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE-RELATED IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES [E1.IRO-1] - Introduction
heading: DESCRIPTION OF THE PR OCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE -RELATED IMPACTS , RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES [E1.IRO -1]
start_phrase: Materiality assessment identified 6 impacts, 10 risks, and 11 opportunities related to climate change.
summary: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s materiality assessment (E1.IRO-1) identified 6 climate-related impacts, 10 risks, and 11 opportunities across its upstream and downstream value chain, covering actual and potential effects over short (≤1 year), medium (≤5 years), and long (>5 years) horizons. Impacts were evaluated by scale, scope, irreversibility, severity, and probability, alongside potential benefits (revenue growth, cost reduction, process optimization). The assessment combined qualitative and quantitative analyses, measuring financial effects via exposed assets relative to the balance sheet and impacts on gross profit, and incorporated client sector data (NACE) and financed clients’ emissions. Findings highlight high exposure to portfolio emissions and significant transition risks in energy‑intensive sectors, making risk/opportunity management critical to long‑term financial stability. Adaptation was deemed important for impacts and opportunities, with related risks moderate to low. Key opportunities include issuing green bonds; financing low‑emission transport (electromobility, charging infrastructure) and technologies; supporting low‑emission construction and rising client demand for related financial products; early entry into energy storage in Poland; and leveraging pro‑transition regulations to gain competitive advantage and support customers’ thermomodernization and low‑emission vehicle purchases.
text:
DESCRIPTION OF THE PR OCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE -RELATED IMPACTS , RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES  [E1.IRO -
1] 
Materiality assessment identified 6 impacts, 10 risks, and 11 opportunities related to climate change. The assessment 
included both actual and potential impacts that may occur in the short, medium, and long term, considering both 
direct and indirect effect s across the value chain (both upstream and downstream). During the identification of 
impacts, the focus was on understanding how the activities of the Bank’s Group and its business relationships affect 
the environment. Each impact was analyzed in terms of  scale, scope, irreversibility, severity, and probability of 
occurrence, with benefits arising from their materialization, such as revenue growth, cost reduction, or operational 
process optimization, also being taken into account.  
The materiality assessme nt also considered the risks and opportunities and their impact on the Bank’s Group. The 
evaluation was based on both qualitative and quantitative analyses. Whenever possible, the distinction between 
materiality in the short -term (within 1 year), medium -term (within 5 years), and long -term (above 5 years) was 
included. Financial impact was measured by the value of exposed assets relative to the Bank’s Group's balance sheet 
and the impact on gross profit. The specificity of the organization and clients finan ced by the Bank (sectoral data 
based on NACE classification), including their emissions, was also considered.  
The high importance of mitigating climate change results from the fact that the Bank’s Group is heavily exposed to 
climate risks associated with emissions in its portfolio. Transition risks are also significant, as many industries that 
the Group finances require a transformation towards a low -emission economy. Managing these risks and associated 
opportunities is crucial for the long -term financial stability of the Bank.  
The high assessment of risks and opportunities related to energy arises from the Group’s exposure to sectors with 
high energy demand. Transformations related to the energy transition, including switching to clean energy sources, 
pose both a risk and a potential opportunity. The Bank’s Group can benefit from supporting sustainable energy 
investments, which align with the global decarbonization trend. Adaptation to climate change was deemed important 
in terms of impacts and opportuniti es, whereas the risks related to this subtopic were assessed as moderate or low. 
This means that the Bank’s Group can focus on developing adaptive actions within its portfolio while managing 
moderate risks associated with the physical impacts of climate ch ange. Identified opportunities offer growth potential, 
especially in the context of supporting sustainable investments, as well as increasing revenue and reducing costs, 
resulting from the implementation of new technologies, more efficient resource managem ent, and the use of new 
markets related to investments in the green economy.  
Eleven opportunities related to climate change were identified, including:  
• Green bonds represent an opportunity for the Bank to raise additional capital to support financing sust ainable 
development and transition to a low -emission economy. Funds raised from the sale of bonds will contribute to 
the development of the "green" part of the Bank’s credit portfolio and the Bank’s Group;  
• Low-emission transport is an important area in terms of reducing the economy’s emissions. The Bank and its 
Group can capitalize on current trends related to the development of electromobility and the use of alternative 
fuels.  The positive trend related to  the development of electromobility requires the development of adequate 
infrastructure to provide charging stations for electric vehicles, which presents an opportunity for the Bank and 
the Bank’s Group;  
• The energy -climate transition involves increasing benefits from conducting low -emission business activities. 
Rising costs of high -emission activities and companies' efforts to reduce emissions present an opportunity for 
the Bank and the Bank’s Group, which can provide financing for the purchase of low -emission technologies;  
• Low-emission construction is an important area in terms of reducing the economy’s emissions. The Bank and the 
Bank’s Group can take advantage of current trends and regulatory requirements related to low -emission building 
construction;  
• Low-emission construction is associated with lower demand for primary energy and energy costs. Seeing the 
above benefits, the Bank and the Bank’s Group can capitalize on the growing demand from clients for financial 
products supporting low -emission constr uction;  
• With the energy transition and the shift towards a low -emission economy, energy storage systems can play an 
important role in ensuring the stability of energy supply and the electricity grid. In Poland, energy storage 
technologies are at an early stage of development and present an opportunity for early market entry;
