heading: Table 50. Template 2 – GAR sector information – Turnover , 2024
start_phrase: Breakdown by sector – 4 digits level (code and label Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) Water and marine resources (WTR) Circular economy (CE) Pollution (PPC) Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO) TOTAL (CCM + CCA + WTR + CE + PPC + BIO)
summary:
- Context: Extract from PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group Director’s Report 2024 presenting EU Taxonomy/Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures.
- Template 2 – GAR sector information – Turnover (2024):
  - Detailed NACE 4-digit sector breakdown of gross carrying amounts (PLN million) for non-financial corporates subject to NFRD and SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD.
  - Allocation across the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - “Of which environmentally sustainable” fields indicate taxonomy-aligned portions by sector and objective.
  - Examples of notable aligned exposures include:
    - D3511 Production of electricity (118.81 total; 59.72 aligned) and D3513 Distribution of electricity (20.76; 14.11).
    - J6130 Satellite telecommunications (47.37; 44.07) spanning CCM/CCA and a small BIO element.
    - C2442 Aluminium production (17.76; 9.45).
    - C2511 Metal structures (22.58; 12.01) and C2512 Metal doors/windows (30.19; 16.07).
    - C2221 Plastic plates/sheets (25.71; 13.69).
    - C2892 Mining/construction machinery (24.35; 24.35).
    - Low or no alignment in sectors such as B0510 Mining of hard coal.
  - Includes instances of CCA-linked manufacturing (e.g., concrete products for construction) and smaller aligned amounts in selected automotive supply-chain activities.
- Template 3 – GAR KPI stock – CapEx (2024):
  - Proportions of total covered assets that are taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned by objective (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO).
  - Breakdown by counterparty class and instrument:
    - Financial undertakings (including insurance), non-financial undertakings, households (notably loans collateralised by residential property and building renovation loans), and local government financing.
    - Instruments: loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds), and equity instruments.
  - “Of which” tags highlight use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Summary line shows totals for GAR assets and the overall proportion of total assets covered by the disclosure (coverage around two thirds of total assets).
- Overall: The section quantifies sectoral turnover and CapEx-related exposures against EU Taxonomy criteria, indicating eligibility/alignment shares and highlighting where the Group’s portfolio contributes to the environmental objectives.

heading: Table 51. Template 3 – GAR KPI stock – CapEx, 2024
start_phrase: a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x z aa ab ac ad ae af
summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Template 3 – GAR KPI stock – CapEx for PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group, with side‑by‑side disclosures for 2024 (reference date T) and 2023 (T‑1).
- Scope covers loans and advances, debt securities (including Use‑of‑Proceeds/green bonds), and equity instruments not held for trading; broken down by counterparty segments: financial undertakings (including insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households (with “of which” for residential mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local government financing, and collateral taken.
- Reports, for both numerator and denominator of the Green Asset Ratio, the proportion of total covered assets that are Taxonomy‑eligible and Taxonomy‑aligned across all six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
- Identifies “of which” categories for Use‑of‑Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities within each environmental objective and segment.
- Provides headline totals:
  - Total Taxonomy‑eligible share of covered assets around 34.6% in 2024 versus about 33.1% in 2023.
  - Total Taxonomy‑aligned share of covered assets around 2.0% in 2024 versus about 1.2% in 2023.
  - Proportion of total assets covered in the GAR denominator is roughly two‑thirds in both years (about 66%).
- Segment highlights indicate high eligibility within households (notably residential mortgage exposures, including a subset of building renovation loans), measurable eligible and aligned shares within non‑financial undertakings, limited alignment within financial undertakings, and negligible contributions from local government financing and repossessed collateral.
- The tables thus provide a structured, year‑over‑year view of the Group’s GAR for CapEx, detailing sectoral and instrument composition, and the split between eligible, aligned, enabling, transitional, and Use‑of‑Proceeds exposures across environmental objectives.

summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPI stock disclosures for PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group:
  - CapEx-based GAR for 2023 (disclosure reference date T-1)
  - Turnover-based GAR for 2024 (disclosure reference date T)
- Scope covers assets included in both numerator and denominator: loans and advances, debt securities, and equity instruments not held for trading.
- Breakdowns provided by counterparty and instrument type:
  - Financial undertakings (including credit institutions, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings)
  - Non-financial undertakings
  - Households (with details for residential mortgage loans, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans)
  - Local government financing and collateral obtained by possession
  - Split into loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds), and equity instruments
- Reports taxonomy-eligible vs taxonomy-aligned shares across EU environmental objectives:
  - Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA)
  - Water and marine resources (WTR)
  - Circular economy (CE)
  - Pollution prevention and control (PPC)
  - Biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO)
- Identifies activity types within exposures:
  - Use-of-proceeds instruments
  - Enabling activities
  - Transitional activities
- Key coverage metric:
  - Proportion of total assets covered by the GAR scope is c. 65%–66% (c. 65.37% for CapEx 2023; c. 65.95% for Turnover 2024).
- High-level observations:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible exposures are in the low-to-mid 30% range of covered assets.
  - Taxonomy-aligned shares are low single digits overall, concentrated mainly in Climate Change Mitigation; alignment for other environmental objectives is minimal.
  - Transitional activity exposure is negligible; enabling and use‑of‑proceeds components are present but small.
  - Household exposures are dominated by residential mortgage lending; building renovation loans are identified separately.
  - Non-financial undertakings carry most of the eligible/aligned potential relative to other segments; financial undertakings show limited alignment, with insurance exposures mainly via debt securities.

- Presents PKO Bank Polski Group’s EU Taxonomy disclosure Template 3 – GAR KPI stock – Turnover for 2024 with a comparative table for 2023.
- Shows the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) composition for covered assets in both numerator and denominator, broken down by counterparty type and instrument: financial undertakings (including insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households, and sub‑items such as credit institutions, investment firms, management companies, local government financing, and collateral obtained.
- Details exposures by instrument class (loans and advances, debt securities including use‑of‑proceeds instruments, equity) and by taxonomy classification “of which” categories: use‑of‑proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- Reports taxonomy alignment and eligibility across all six environmental objectives: climate change mitigation and adaptation, water and marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Highlights households—especially loans collateralised by residential immovable property—and building renovation loans as separately reported categories; motor vehicle loans and local‑government‑related items are negligible.
- For financial undertakings, insurance‑related exposures (notably via debt securities) are specifically itemised; many other financial subcategories show zero/negligible values.
- For non‑financial undertakings, both loan and debt‑security exposures are shown with enabling/use‑of‑proceeds shares.
- Provides totals indicating:
  - Proportion of total assets covered by the GAR: ~65.95% in 2024 vs ~65.37% in 2023.
  - Total taxonomy‑aligned share of covered assets: ~34.21% in 2024 vs ~32.39% in 2023.
- Overall, the section evidences a slight year‑on‑year increase in both GAR coverage and taxonomy‑aligned exposures, with mortgage lending dominating the covered asset base and detailed granularity on enabling/use‑of‑proceeds activities.

summary:
- This section of the PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group Director’s Report 2024 presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) key performance indicators, using EBA/Taxonomy templates for both stock (2023, reference date T-1) and flow (2024 CapEx, reference date T).
- Template 3 – GAR KPI stock – Turnover, 2023:
  - Shows the proportion of total covered assets included in both the numerator and denominator of the GAR.
  - Breaks down exposures by counterparty type (financial undertakings, credit institutions, other financial corporations, insurance undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households, local government) and by instrument (loans and advances, debt securities including use-of-proceeds, equity instruments, collateral obtained).
  - Discloses “of which” categories for use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Provides taxonomy-eligible vs taxonomy-aligned shares by environmental objective: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular economy (CE), Pollution prevention and control (PPC), and Biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
  - Highlights include: very high coverage in household exposures, especially mortgages (near 100% coverage of loans collateralised by residential property), explicit identification of building renovation loans, and minimal/marginal contributions from motor vehicle loans and local government financing.
  - Aggregate figures indicate a substantial portion of covered assets are taxonomy-eligible, with a lower subset taxonomy-aligned; alignment is concentrated in climate objectives.
- Template 4 – GAR KPI flow – CapEx, 2024:
  - Reports the GAR for new assets/capex during the reporting period (flow metric).
  - Uses the same sectoral and product breakdown and the same “of which” classifications (use-of-proceeds, transitional, enabling).
  - Provides taxonomy-eligible vs taxonomy-aligned proportions by environmental objective, showing that most alignment is in Climate Change Mitigation and, to a lesser extent, Climate Change Adaptation, with very small shares for WTR, CE, PPC, and BIO.
  - Presents overall totals for flow: around half of new covered assets are taxonomy-eligible and a smaller portion is taxonomy-aligned.
- Overall, the pages quantify the bank’s EU Taxonomy exposure and alignment profile across sectors and products, distinguishing stock (2023) from flow (2024 CapEx), and detailing the role of enabling/transitional activities and use-of-proceeds instruments.

title: IDENTIFICATION OF ENTITIES SUBJECT TO DIRECTIVE 2013/34/EU
heading: IDENTIFICATION OF ENT ITIES SUBJECT TO DIRECTIVE 2013/34/EU
start_phrase: The Bank has conducted an analysis of its portfolio with re spect to customers obligated to disclose sustainability - related information in accordance with the criteria specified in Articles 19a or 29a of Directive 2013/34/EU, including mandatory disclosures under the EU Taxonomy.
summary:
- Focuses on PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s EU Taxonomy disclosures and methodology for 2024, including consolidated key performance indicators (KPIs) for taxonomy-aligned activities.
- States that Table 61 presents a consolidated KPI at Group level as a revenue-weighted average across segments; the Group operates in banking and asset management, with leasing and factoring treated similarly to lending.
- Clarifies the Group is not a financial conglomerate under the Polish Act of 15 April 2005, but prepares a consolidated sustainability report with taxonomy disclosures using a prudential consolidation approach.
- Explains KPI calculation per Commission Notice (EU) C/2024/6691: the Group publishes a consolidated KPI and, for prudentially consolidated subsidiaries, KPI Turnover and KPI CapEx, weighted by each activity’s share of total consolidated revenue.
- Describes the scope and data sources for taxonomy disclosures: company non-financial reports, the Notoria ESG Module (for Polish companies’ non-financial data), and the EMIS platform (to map parent–subsidiary structures and identify consolidated entities financed by the Group).
- Details identification of clients subject to Directive 2013/34/EU (Articles 19a and 29a): large public-interest entities with >500 employees and parent PIEs of large groups (including their consolidated subsidiaries).
- Outlines the method to assess compliance with EU Taxonomy minimum safeguards (Article 18): review of Notoria data (e.g., OECD principle violations), cross-check with company reports, and expert judgment to classify entities as meeting (YES) or not meeting (NO) minimum safeguards.
- Notes that activities of entities not meeting minimum safeguards are disclosed as taxonomy-eligible but not taxonomy-aligned.
- Applies a group-level assumption: if a parent company reports compliance with minimum safeguards, all its consolidated subsidiaries are deemed compliant; this approach stands until sector-wide verification guidelines are developed.
- States the Group does not verify minimum safeguards for retail customers in real estate lending.
- Provides contextual information on the scope of assets/activities covered by KPIs and indicates reliance on available public and database sources, acknowledging the interim nature of methods pending unified sector guidance.
text:
The Bank has conducted an analysis of its portfolio with re spect to customers obligated to disclose sustainability -
related information in accordance with the criteria specified in Articles 19a or 29a of Directive 2013/34/EU, including 
mandatory disclosures under the EU Taxonomy. They include:  
• Large entities that a re public -interest entities, exceeding the threshold of an average of 500 employees during 
the financial year as of the balance sheet date;  
• Public -interest entities that are parent companies of large groups, exceeding the threshold of an average of 500 
employees during the financial year on a consolidated basis as of the balance sheet date, as well as the 
subsidiaries consolidated by these parent companies.   
As part of the customer verification process, the Bank relied on the most up -to-date non -financial  reports published 
by companies subject to Directive 2013/34/EU, which were available on the websites of the analysed companies. The 
customer verification also used information available in the Notoria ESG Module database, which contains data 
resulting fro m the non -financial reporting obligations of Polish companies.  
To identify subsidiaries financed by capital groups formed by parent companies, the Bank uses the EMIS information 
and analytical platform. This database displays the relationships and lists o f subsidiaries subject to consolidation by 
the parent company for each capital group.  
By utilizing data gathered in the Bank's information system and data from the EMIS database, the Bank compiled a 
list of subsidiaries consolidated by the parent companie s of capital groups that have received financing from the 
Bank’s Group.

title: METHOD OF ASSESSING COMPLIANCE WITH MINIMUM SAFEGUARDS
heading: METHOD OF ASSESSING C OMPLIANCE WITH MINIM UM SAFEGUARDS
start_phrase: The verification of compliance with the minimum safeguards specified in Article 18 of the EU Taxonomy by non - financial and finan cial enterprises subject to Directive 2013/34/EU is based on data obtained from the Notoria ESG Module database and information contained in the non -financial reports of these customers.
summary:
- Presents PKO Bank Polski Group’s approach to EU Taxonomy disclosures for 2024, including a consolidated key performance indicator calculated as a revenue-weighted average across segments (banking and asset management), with leasing and factoring treated like lending.
- Confirms the Group is not a financial conglomerate; taxonomy disclosures follow a prudential consolidation approach and the Commission Notice (EU) C/2024/6691 methodology.
- Describes scope, data sources, and limitations: entities subject to Directive 2013/34/EU identified via company non-financial reports, the Notoria ESG Module, and the EMIS platform to map parent–subsidiary structures and compile financed subsidiaries.
- Details minimum safeguards verification (Article 18): uses Notoria ESG data (e.g., OECD violations) and companies’ non-financial reports; applies expert judgment to assign YES/NO; if a parent meets safeguards, all its consolidated subsidiaries are assumed to meet them; banks do not verify safeguards for retail real estate customers per EC guidance and the Sustainable Finance Platform.
- Explains taxonomy eligibility/alignment assessment for exposures to financial and non-financial entities under the Directive using disclosed Turnover and CapEx KPIs (2024 reports for 2023 data), with a hierarchy: subsidiary KPI; if unavailable, closest parent KPI; if still unavailable, consolidated group KPI; for financial institutions, apply at parent level.
- For banking book exposures with unknown use of proceeds, taxonomy-eligible/aligned amounts are calculated as gross carrying amount multiplied by the relevant KPIs; earmarked financing not reported as aligned due to insufficient technical screening data.
- Addresses off-balance-sheet items: financial guarantees not disclosed due to immateriality; exposures related to managed assets via a Group subsidiary and other off-balance exposures to non-financial entities are assessed using Turnover and CapEx KPIs.
- Classifies household renovation loans as taxonomy-eligible but not aligned due to lack of technical screening evidence.
- Classifies residential mortgage exposures as taxonomy-eligible and potentially aligned if they meet substantial contribution to climate change mitigation and DNSH for adaptation (activity 7.7), evidenced by energy performance certificates.
- Provides national thresholds for energy performance: for buildings before 31 Dec 2020, EP < 83.91 kWh/(m2*yr) single-family and < 81.86 kWh/(m2*yr) multi-family; for buildings after that date, EP at least 10% below NZEB limits (63 and 58.5 kWh/(m2*yr) respectively) per Polish regulations.
text:
The verification of compliance with the minimum safeguards specified in Article 18 of the EU Taxonomy by non -
financial and finan cial enterprises subject to Directive 2013/34/EU is based on data obtained from the Notoria ESG 
Module database and information contained in the non -financial reports of these customers. The verification consists 
of analyzing data from Notoria, including t he occurrence of violations of OECD principles, and cross -referencing these 
results with information found in the non -financial reports. The final step involves comparing the collected data, upon 
which expert judgment is applied, assigning a "YES" marker t o businesses that meet the minimum safeguards or a 
"NO" marker to businesses that do not meet the minimum safeguards. Economic activities of non -financial and 
financial enterprises subject to Directive 2013/34/EU that do not meet the minimum safeguards are  disclosed as 
taxonomy -eligible but not taxonomy -aligned.  
The Bank assumes that all subsidiaries consolidated by the parent company of a given capital group have been 
considered in the assessment of compliance with the minimum safeguards in relation to th e activities conducted by 
the group. If the parent company publishes information on meeting the minimum safeguards, the Bank assumes that 
all subsidiaries consolidated by the parent company also meet the minimum safeguards.  
The verification method describ ed above remains in effect until the banking sector develops uniform 
guidelines/explanations/recommendations on how to verify the minimum safeguards based on sustainability reports.  
The Bank’s Group does not verify compliance with the minimum safeguards fo r retail customers in relation to real 
estate purchases. According to the third notification from the European Commission (C/2024/6691), credit THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP

 institutions should obtain documentation confirming compliance with the relevant technical qualification criteri a and 
minimum safeguards from producers supplying goods and services to retail customers. However, the notification 
does not state that this applies to real estate purchases. Furthermore, the Sustainable Finance Platform holds that 
households are not subje ct to the minimum safeguards, which apply to businesses or local governments, and 
therefore, banks are not required to obtain information on compliance with the minimum safeguards from households 
when providing mortgage loans or other types of financing.

title: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBILITY FOR AND ALIGNMENT WITH THE TAXONOMY OF EXPOSURES TO FINANCIAL AND NON-FINANCIAL ENTITIES SUBJECT TO DIRECTIVE 2013/34/EU
heading: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBI LITY FOR AND ALIGNME NT WITH THE TAXONOMY OF EXPOSURES TO FIN ANCIAL AND NON -FINANCIAL ENTITIES S UBJECT TO DIRECTIVE 2013/34/EU
start_phrase: To determine the exposure to financial and non - financial entities subject to Directive 2013/34/EU and their subsidiaries consolidated by the parent company of a given capital group, classified as taxonomy -eligible and taxonomy -aligned, the Bank used key performance indicators (KPIs) of Turnover and CapEx.
summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpt from PKO Bank Polski Group’s 2024 Director’s Report detailing EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment assessments across exposures, with regulatory interpretations and data sources.

- Minimum safeguards and documentation:
  - Institutions should obtain documentation from producers to confirm compliance with technical qualification criteria for goods/services to retail customers, but this does not apply to real estate purchases.
  - The Sustainable Finance Platform indicates households are not subject to minimum safeguards; therefore, banks need not collect minimum-safeguards information from households for mortgages or similar financing.

- Methodology for entities subject to Directive 2013/34/EU:
  - Taxonomy eligibility and alignment assessed using Turnover and CapEx KPIs disclosed in 2024 for 2023 non-financial reports.
  - Subsidiary treatment: apply the KPI disclosed by the parent for that subsidiary; if unavailable, use the closest parent’s KPI; if still unavailable, use the group’s consolidated KPI. All subsidiaries consolidated by the parent are assumed included. For financial institutions, apply at the parent level.
  - For banking book exposures with unknown purpose (loans, advances, debt securities, equity instruments), taxonomy-eligible/aligned values are calculated as gross carrying amount multiplied by the relevant Turnover/CapEx KPI.
  - Earmarked financing not reported as taxonomy-eligible/aligned due to insufficient data confirming compliance with technical screening criteria.
  - Off-balance-sheet guarantees linked to taxonomy-aligned financing are not disclosed due to immateriality.
  - Managed assets aligned with the taxonomy relate to a group subsidiary; off-balance-sheet exposures to non-financial entities under the Directive are assessed via Turnover/CapEx KPIs.

- Household exposures and taxonomy assessment:
  - Renovation loans to households are taxonomy-eligible but not aligned due to lack of evidence of compliance with technical screening criteria (sections 7.2–7.6 of Annex I to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139).
  - Residential property loans can be taxonomy-eligible and aligned if they meet substantial contribution to climate change mitigation and comply with “do no significant harm” for climate change adaptation (section 7.7 of Annex I).
  - National interpretation (Poland) for substantial contribution thresholds:
    - Buildings constructed before 31 Dec 2020: EP (non-renewable primary energy demand) must be below 83.91 kWh/(m2*year) for single-family and below 81.86 kWh/(m2*year) for multi-family, evidenced by an energy performance certificate.
    - Buildings constructed after 31 Dec 2020: EP must be at least 10% lower than the national NZEB threshold; the bank applies reduced limit values of 63 kWh/(m2*year) for single-family and 58.5 kWh/(m2*year) for multi-family, per national technical regulations.
text:
ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBI LITY FOR AND ALIGNME NT WITH THE TAXONOMY  OF EXPOSURES TO FIN ANCIAL AND NON -FINANCIAL ENTITIES S UBJECT TO 
DIRECTIVE 2013/34/EU   
To determine the exposure to financial and non -financial entities subject to Directive 2013/34/EU and their 
subsidiaries consolidated by the parent company of a given capital group, classified as taxonomy -eligible and 
taxonomy -aligned, the Bank used key performance indicators (KPIs) of Turnover and CapEx. These indicators were 
disclosed by entities required to r eport non -financial information in non -financial reports published in 2024 (for the 
year 2023).  
For subsidiaries of the capital group created by the parent company, the Bank applied the following key: exposures 
to subsidiaries are multiplied by the key pe rformance indicator disclosed by the parent company for that subsidiary; 
if the key performance indicator of the subsidiary is not available, the KPIs of the closest parent company are used; 
if the KPI of the closest parent company is unavailable, the cons olidated KPI at the capital group level is used. The 
Bank assumes that all subsidiaries consolidated by the parent company are considered when calculating 
consolidated KPIs. For financial institutions, the indicator is applied at the parent company level. For exposures in the 
banking portfolio, where the purpose of funds is unknown (loans and advances, debt securities, and equity 
instruments), the value of taxonomy -eligible and taxonomy -aligned assets is calculated as the product of the gross 
carrying amoun t and the appropriate KPIs: Turnover KPI and CapEx KPI.  
The Bank did not report exposures that are taxonomy -eligible and taxonomy -aligned in terms of earmarked financing 
due to the lack of data to confirm compliance with the technical qualification criteri a of the EU Taxonomy for the 
financed investment project.  
Regarding off -balance -sheet exposures, the Bank does not disclose  financial guarantees supporting loans and 
advances and debt securities financing business activities that are taxonomy -aligned  due to their immateriality.  
Exposures related to managed assets coming from enterprises financing business activities aligned with the 
taxonomy concern a subsidiary of the Bank’s Capital Group. Off -balance -sheet exposures to non -financial entities 
subject to D irective 2013/34/EU are assessed as taxonomy -eligible and taxonomy -aligned based on the Turnover 
KPI and CapEx KPI. These KPIs were disclosed in non -financial reports published in 2024 (for the year 2023).

title: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBILITY FOR AND COMPLIANCE WITH THE TAXONOMY OF EXPOSURES TO HOUSEHOLDS
heading: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBI LITY FOR AND COMPLIA NCE WITH THE TAXONOMY OF EXPO SURES TO HOUSEHOLDS
start_phrase: Exposures to households arising from loans for building renovations have been classified as taxonomy -eligible but not taxonomy -aligned due to the lack of data confirming compliance with the technical screening criter ia (concerning activities under sections 7.2, 7.3, 7.4, 7.5, and 7.6, as defined in Annex I to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139).
summary:
- The report details PKO Bank Polski’s application of the EU Taxonomy to its exposures, clarifying that households are not subject to minimum safeguards; therefore, the bank does not collect minimum-safeguard data from retail clients for mortgages or similar financing.
- Methodology for entities under Directive 2013/34/EU: taxonomy eligibility and alignment are assessed using Turnover and CapEx KPIs disclosed in 2024 for 2023. A hierarchy applies KPIs from the subsidiary, nearest parent, or consolidated group; for financial institutions, KPIs are applied at the parent level.
- For banking book exposures with unknown use of proceeds (loans, debt securities, equity), taxonomy-eligible/aligned values are calculated as gross carrying amount multiplied by the relevant KPI(s).
- The bank did not report earmarked/specialized financing as taxonomy-eligible/aligned due to insufficient data to confirm technical screening criteria; financial guarantees were not disclosed due to immateriality. Managed assets exposures via a subsidiary were assessed using the same KPI approach. Off-balance exposures to non-financial entities use Turnover/CapEx KPIs.
- Households:
  - Renovation loans: taxonomy-eligible but not aligned because technical screening evidence is lacking (EU 2021/2139 sections 7.2–7.6).
  - Residential property loans: taxonomy-eligible and potentially aligned under section 7.7 if substantial contribution to climate change mitigation and DNSH for adaptation are met.
  - Energy performance criteria: 
    - Buildings before 31 Dec 2020: EP <83.91 kWh/(m²*year) for single-family; <81.86 for multi-family, confirmed by EPC.
    - Buildings after 31 Dec 2020: EP at least 10% below NZEB thresholds (63 kWh/(m²*year) single-family; 58.5 multi-family), confirmed by EPC.
  - DNSH for adaptation verified via KLIMADA 2.0 physical risk analysis, requiring risk <0.75 over the loan’s maturity.
  - Vehicle loans: not reported as taxonomy-eligible due to lack of detailed asset data (section 6.5).
- Local governments: the bank’s model is not focused on public housing; it does not disclose exposures financing public housing and did not report taxonomy-eligible specialized lending due to insufficient project-level data.
- Repossessed real estate collateral: no such exposures reported.
- Green Asset Ratio (GAR) drivers: the largest contribution comes from household residential real estate and general corporate exposures to non-financial enterprises (assessed via published KPIs), primarily supporting the climate change mitigation objective. Building alignment checks follow section 7.7 of EU 2021/2139.
- Non-reported taxonomy-aligned areas due to data gaps: targeted corporate financing (project-level), household renovation loans, household vehicle loans, and specialized lending to local governments.
- Strategy and compliance integration: the 2025–2027 Strategy sets a goal to be the leading financier of Poland’s energy transition (>20% market share), focusing on low-emission energy, low-emission buildings, and zero-emission vehicle financing.
- Climate commitments: net-zero across all scopes by 2050, with near-term actions including reducing own emissions via infrastructure/efficiency (Scope 1) and sourcing at least 90% of electricity from renewables (Scope 2).
text:
Exposures to households arising from loans for building renovations have been classified as taxonomy -eligible but 
not taxonomy -aligned due to the lack of data confirming compliance with the technical screening criter ia (concerning 
activities under sections 7.2, 7.3, 7.4, 7.5, and 7.6, as defined in Annex I to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139).  
Exposures to households arising from loans for residential properties have been classified as taxonomy -eligible and 
taxonom y-aligned, provided they meet the condition of making a substantial contribution to climate change mitigation 
and the "do no significant harm" principle in relation to climate change adaptation (concerning activities under section 
7.7 of Annex I to Delegat ed Regulation (EU) 2021/2139).  
According to the interpretation of the Ministry of Development and Technology, the assessment of the substantial 
contribution to climate change mitigation for residential buildings constructed before 31 December 2020 is met w hen 
the demand for non -renewable primary energy for heating, ventilation, cooling, and hot water preparation (EP 
indicator) is lower than 83.91 kWh/(m2*year) for single -family residential buildings and lower than 81.86 
kWh/(m2*year) for multi -family reside ntial buildings, as confirmed by the building's energy performance certificate.  
According to the interpretation of the Ministry of Development and Technology, the assessment of a significant 
contribution to climate change mitigation for residential buildin gs constructed after 31 December 2020 is met when 
the EP indicator is at least 10% lower than the threshold set for the nearly zero -energy building (NZEB) requirements 
in national measures implementing Directive 2010/31/EU of the European Parliament and of  the Council. To this end, 
the Bank compared the calculated value of the EP indicator with the limit value, reduced by 10% (determined as set 
out in § 329(1) of the Announcement of the Minister of Infrastructure of 12 April 2002 on the technical conditions  to 
be met by buildings and their location), of 63 kWh/(m2*year) for single -family residential buildings and 58.5 THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP  
DIRECTOR’S REPORT FOR 2024  
prepared jointly with the PKO Bank Polski S.A Director’s Report   
 
 Strona 226/288 
 
 
 kWh/(m2*year) for multi -family buildings. The EP value was confirmed by the building's energy performance 
certificate.  
The "do no significant  harm" principle in relation to the environmental objective of climate change adaptation was 
confirmed through an analysis of the physical risk exposure of the properties under consideration using the KLIMADA 
2.0 portal, based on the property address, for which the risk level was found to be less than 0.75 (within the time 
horizon corresponding to the maturity of the loan).  
The Bank did not report exposures classified as taxonomy -eligible for households arising from loans for vehicles due 
to the lack of detailed information regarding the financed object (concerning activities under section 6.5 of Annex I to 
Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139).

title: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBILITY FOR AND COMPLIANCE WITH THE TAXONOMY OF EXPOSURES TO LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS
heading: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBI LITY FOR AND COMPLIA NCE WITH THE TAXONOM Y OF EXPOSURES TO LO CAL GOVERNMENT UNITS
start_phrase: PKO Bank P olski S.A. is a universal bank and its business model is not based on the financing of public housing.
summary:
- Focus on EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment of PKO Bank Polski’s exposures, with emphasis on methodology, data limitations, and disclosure scope.
- Energy performance for multi-family buildings verified via energy performance certificates (EP kWh/m2/year); “do no significant harm” for climate change adaptation assessed using KLIMADA 2.0, requiring physical risk <0.75 over loan maturity.
- No taxonomy-eligible reporting for household vehicle loans due to insufficient object-level data (EU Taxonomy section 6.5).
- Local government units: as a universal bank not centered on public housing, the Bank does not disclose such exposures and reported no taxonomy-eligible specialized lending to public authorities due to lack of eligibility/alignment data.
- No reported exposures from repossessed commercial or residential real estate collateral.
- Green Asset Ratio (GAR) driven mainly by:
  - Household exposures financing residential real estate.
  - General financing to non-financial enterprises subject to Directive 2013/34/EU, using KPIs from their non-financial reports.
  - Activities primarily contribute to the climate change mitigation (CCM) objective; residential real estate alignment verified under Section 7.7 (Acquisition and ownership of buildings) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139.
- Areas not reported as taxonomy-aligned due to data gaps: targeted corporate financing, household renovation loans, household vehicle loans, and LGU financing for non-residential public housing.
- Integration with strategy, product design, and client engagement: 2025–2027 Strategy aims to become “Number 1” in financing Poland’s energy transition with >20% market share, focusing on low-emission energy, low-emission buildings, and zero-emission vehicles; commitments include >20% share in transition financing and achieving net-zero by 2050 across all scopes, with actions on Scope 1 (infrastructure modernization, building energy efficiency) and Scope 2 (at least 90% renewable electricity).
text:
PKO Bank P olski S.A. is a universal bank and its business model is not based on the financing of public housing. The 
Bank does not disclose exposures to local authority units for loans and advances that finance public housing. The 
Bank did not report exposures class ified as taxonomy -eligible to public authorities related to specialised lending due 
to the lack of information on the eligibility and alignment with the taxonomy of the financed investment projects.

heading: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBI LITY FOR AND ALIGNME NT WITH THE TAX ONOMY OF REPOSSESSED COMMERCIAL AND RESI DENTIAL REAL ESTATE COLLATERAL

summary:

title: DESCRIPTION OF THE COMPLIANCE WITH REGULATION (EU) 2020/852 IN THE FINANCIAL UNDERTAKING’S BUSINESS STRATEGY, PRODUCT DESIGN PROCESSES AND ENGAGEMENT WITH CLIENTS AND COUNTERPARTIES
heading: DESCRIPTION OF THE CO MPLIANCE WITH REGULATION (EU) 2020/852 IN THE FINANCIAL UN DERTAKING ’S BUSINESS STRATEGY , PRODUCT DESIGN PROCE SSES AND ENGAGEMENT WITH CLIENTS AND COU NTERPARTIES
start_phrase: In October 2024, the Bank’s Management Board adopted the Strategy for the years 2025 -2027, which defined seven main pillars outlining the goals of the Bank's Group.
summary:
- Scope and methodology for EU Taxonomy assessments:
  - For residential real estate, energy performance (EP) values for multi-family buildings are confirmed via energy performance certificates.
  - DNSH for climate change adaptation is assessed using the KLIMADA 2.0 portal; properties must show physical risk <0.75 over the loan maturity horizon.
  - No reporting of taxonomy-eligible household vehicle loans due to insufficient data (EU 2021/2139, section 6.5).

- Exposures to public sector and collateral:
  - The Bank’s model is not focused on financing public housing; it does not disclose exposures for such loans to local authorities.
  - No taxonomy-eligible specialized lending to public authorities reported due to lack of data on eligibility/alignment of financed projects.
  - No reported exposures related to repossessed commercial or residential real estate collateral.

- Taxonomy-aligned activities and GAR/BTAR drivers:
  - The largest share of GAR comes from:
    - Household exposures financing residential real estate, and
    - General financing of non-financial enterprises subject to Directive 2013/34/EU, based on KPIs in their non-financial reports.
  - Reported taxonomy-aligned activities primarily support climate change mitigation.
  - Residential real estate alignment assessed per Annex I, Section 7.7 (Acquisition and ownership of buildings).
  - Not reported as taxonomy-aligned due to data gaps:
    - Targeted financing for non-financial enterprises (lack of technical screening evidence),
    - Household loans for building renovations,
    - Household vehicle loans,
    - Specialist financing for local governments (non-residential public housing).

- Strategy and commitments under Regulation (EU) 2020/852:
  - Strategy 2025–2027 sets a pillar to be “Number 1” in financing Poland’s energy transition with >20% market share, focusing on:
    - Low-emission energy,
    - Low-emission buildings,
    - Zero-emission vehicles.
  - Net-zero by 2050 across Scopes 1–3:
    - Scope 1: reduce own emissions via infrastructure upgrades and building energy efficiency,
    - Scope 2: at least 90% electricity from renewables,
    - Scope 3: transformation plans covering >50% of the credit portfolio by end-2027.
  - Product and process enhancements:
    - Expanded offering including green guarantees (KUKE S.A.) to support clients’ competitiveness and EU Green Deal objectives.
    - June 2024: updated Group-wide “Principles of classification of sustainable development financing,” aligning product taxonomy with EU Taxonomy and European Green Bond; ongoing business, reporting, and IT implementation.
    - Oct 2024: introduced Sustainability-Linked Loans (SLL) for syndicated corporate financing per SLL Principles; additional sustainable products in development.
    - Dec 2024: new regulation to assess compliance with minimum safeguards and due diligence on human rights; coverage includes anti-corruption, taxation, competition, STI, and labor/human rights; process rollout planned.
    - 2024: implemented taxonomy questionnaires to test technical screening compliance in targeted financing; supports client analysis, classification of sustainable assets, and feeds GAR/BTAR. Work ongoing to flag qualifying/aligned exposures (including supporting and transition activities) and to scale ESG data/IT infrastructure.

- Internal classification of sustainable finance (H1 2024):
  - Light green exposures: support sustainable development with positive environmental/social impact; included in BTAR.
  - Dark green exposures: taxonomy-aligned per Article 3 of the EU Taxonomy; included in GAR.
text:
DESCRIPTION OF THE CO MPLIANCE WITH REGULATION (EU)  2020/852  IN THE FINANCIAL UN DERTAKING ’S BUSINESS STRATEGY , 
PRODUCT DESIGN PROCE SSES AND ENGAGEMENT WITH CLIENTS AND COU NTERPARTIES  
In October 2024, the Bank’s  Management Board adopted the Strategy for the years 2025 -2027, which defined seven 
main pillars outlining the goals of the Bank's Group. One of these pillars is to become the "Number 1" in financing the 
energy transition, aiming for a market share of over  20% in banking financing, focusing on the following activities:  
1. Financing low -emission energy;  
2. Financing low -emission buildings;  
3. Financing the purchase and leasing of zero -emission vehicles.  
In the 2025 -2027 Strategy, the Bank declared:  
4. A market share of  over 20% in the financing of Poland's energy transition;   
5. Achieving net -zero emissions by 2050 across all emission scopes in accordance with the Paris Agreement:  
✓ Reducing own emissions through infrastructure modernization and investments in technologies that 
improve the energy efficiency of buildings (Scope 1);  
✓ Using at least 90% electricity from renewable energy sources (Scope 2);  THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP  
DIRECTOR’S REPORT FOR 2024  
prepared jointly with the PKO Bank Polski S.A Director’s Report   
 
 Strona 227/288 
 
 
 ✓ Covering more than 50% of the credit portfolio with a transformation plan by the end of 2027 (Scope 3).  
The product offering of the Bank's Group is being adjusted to the changing needs of its clients and is progressively 
expanding with both proprietary solutions and solutions developed in cooperation with other institutions (e.g., green 
guarantees from the K orporacja Ubezpieczeń Kredytów Eksportowych S.A.), to support the competitiveness of Polish 
companies in the face of rising energy prices and changing business and regulatory requirements. These measures 
are intended to help redirect capital towards activi ties that will significantly contribute to the achievement of European 
Green Deal goals such as climate neutrality and resilience, zero emissions, protection of biodiversity and ecosystems, 
transition to a circular economy and sustainable use of water and marine resources.  
In June 2024, as part of the review and update of internal procedures, the Bank amended the “Principles of 
classification of sustainable development financing in the PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group”, which introduce, alongside 
the classificat ion of sustainable development financing, a uniform classification of products financing sustainable 
development. The principles take into account the requirements of international standards and the regulatory 
environment, in particular those arising from the EU Taxonomy and the European Green Bond. The Bank is in the 
process of implementing the provisions of the Principles, in particular with regard to its business and reporting 
processes, as well as the related IT systems.  
In October 2024, the Bank intro duced a Sustainability -Linked Loan (SLL) product into its corporate client segment 
within syndicated financing, developed based on the principles and guidelines of the Sustainability -Linked Loan 
Principles (SLLP). Work is currently underway on the implemen tation of additional products designed to support 
sustainable development financing, both in the corporate segment and for businesses and enterprises.  
 In December 2024, the Bank introduced a regulation regarding the assessment of compliance with minimum 
safeguards and the implementation of a due diligence mechanism in assessing the negative impact of activities on 
human rights within the minimum safeguards by the Bank’s clients and counterparties. The assessment of compliance 
with minimum safeguards will be linked to the examination of areas such as: anti -corruption, taxation, fair 
competition, science, technology and innovation, as well as human rights and labour rights.  The Bank is currently 
planning the implementation of a process to evaluate complianc e with minimum safeguards within its internal banking 
processes.  
In 2024, the Bank implemented taxonomy questionnaires, which are crucial for assessing compliance with the 
technical screening criteria of the EU Taxonomy in targeted financing. The question naires form the basis for obtaining 
information from the Bank’s customers regarding the minimum requirements that financed investments should meet 
in order to be considered environmentally sustainable. The questionnaires are used to determine/classify sust ainable 
assets. The Bank offers assistance to customers in analyzing taxonomy transactions, which helps customers better 
understand the requirements and benefits associated with implementing sustainable development principles in their 
business. The data ob tained through the taxonomy questionnaires, along with KPI indicators collected from the non -
financial/sustainability reports of clients obligated to report under the Taxonomy, form the basis for calculating the 
Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and the Banking Book  Taxonomy Alignment Ratio (BTAR). The Bank is working on identifying 
(flagging) credit exposures that qualify for taxonomy alignment, are taxonomy -aligned, and relate to financing 
supporting activities, transition activities, or specialized financing. Simu ltaneously, the Bank is adapting its 
infrastructure and IT tools, which will enable the collection, analysis, development, and aggregation of an increasing 
amount of ESG data. This is in response to the growing scope of the Bank's reporting obligations in the coming years.

heading: ADDITIONAL OR COMPLEM ENTARY INFORMATION I N SUPPORT OF THE FIN ANCIAL UNDERTAKING ’S STRATEGIES AND THE WEIGHT OF THE FINANCING OF TAXONOMY -ALIGNED ECONOMIC ACT IVITIES IN THEIR OVE RALL ACTIVITY
start_phrase: In the credit portfolio classification principl es adopted by the Bank's Management Board in the first half of 2024, the Bank distinguished two classes of exposures that finance activities in the fields of environmental protection, social policy, and corporate governance.
summary:
- Strategic transition target: cover over 50% of the credit portfolio with client transformation plans by end-2027 (Scope 3 financed emissions).
- Product and partnership expansion to support the EU Green Deal: adjusting offerings (including green guarantees with Korporacja Ubezpieczeń Kredytów Eksportowych S.A.) to help clients manage rising energy costs and regulatory change and to channel capital toward climate neutrality, resilience, biodiversity protection, circular economy, and sustainable water/marine use.
- Governance and classification updates (June 2024): revised Principles of classification of sustainable development financing introducing a uniform product classification aligned with the EU Taxonomy and the European Green Bond framework; ongoing implementation in business, reporting, and IT systems.
- New sustainable finance products (October 2024 onward): launch of Sustainability-Linked Loans for syndicated corporate financing per SLL Principles; work underway on additional sustainable products for corporate, business, and enterprise segments.
- Minimum safeguards due diligence (December 2024): new regulation to assess clients’ and counterparties’ compliance with minimum safeguards (anti-corruption, taxation, fair competition, science/tech/innovation, human and labor rights); planned integration into internal banking processes.
- EU Taxonomy operationalization (2024): rollout of taxonomy questionnaires to test technical screening criteria in targeted financing; bank support for client analyses; data used to calculate Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and Banking Book Taxonomy Alignment Ratio (BTAR); ongoing flagging of eligible/aligned/supporting/transition/specialized finance exposures and enhancement of ESG data infrastructure and IT tools for expanding reporting needs.
- Internal portfolio classification: 
  - Light green (supporting sustainable development; positive environmental/social impact; included in BTAR; linked to Article 9 objectives).
  - Dark green (taxonomy-aligned per Article 3; included in GAR).
- Growth ambition: increase the share of taxonomy-aligned and supporting-sustainable-development loans, including SLLs, SLBs, eco-friendly loans (RES, electromobility, energy-efficient real estate), and “Własny Kąt” green mortgages aligned with the Green Covered Bond Framework; quantitative details referenced in capital adequacy disclosures (Template 10).
- Energy sector disclosures: reporting of exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities using both CapEx KPI and Turnover KPI approaches for entities under Directive 2013/34/EU, covering stock KPIs and 2024 flow (new originations):
  - CapEx-based: nuclear R&D (NO); construction/operation of new nuclear (YES); operation of existing nuclear (YES). Fossil gas electricity, CHP, and heat generation (all YES).
  - Turnover-based: nuclear R&D (NO); new nuclear (NO); existing nuclear (YES). Fossil gas electricity, CHP, and heat generation (all YES).
text:
ADDITIONAL OR COMPLEM ENTARY INFORMATION I N SUPPORT OF THE FIN ANCIAL UNDERTAKING ’S STRATEGIES AND THE  WEIGHT OF 
THE FINANCING OF TAXONOMY -ALIGNED ECONOMIC ACT IVITIES IN THEIR OVE RALL ACTIVITY  
In the credit portfolio classification principl es adopted by the Bank's Management Board in the first half of 2024, the 
Bank distinguished two classes of exposures that finance activities in the fields of environmental protection, social 
policy, and corporate governance. These are: the class of exposur es supporting sustainable development – light green 
exposures, which relate to financing business activities with a positive environmental impact, particularly contributing 
to the achievement of the environmental objectives described in Article 9 of the EU  Taxonomy, and financing activities 
with a positive impact on society and communities (exposures included in the calculation of the Banking Book 
Taxonomy Alignment Ratio (BTAR)); and the class of environmentally sustainable exposures (taxonomy -aligned) – 
dark green exposures, which relate to financing business activities that meet the criteria described in Article 3 of the 
EU Taxonomy (exposures included in the calculation of the Green Asset Ratio (GAR)).  THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP  
DIRECTOR’S REPORT FOR 2024  
prepared jointly with the PKO Bank Polski S.A Director’s Report   
 
 Strona 228/288 
 
 
 The Bank's Group aims to increase the share of loans  in its banking portfolio that finance business activities meeting 
the criteria outlined in Article 3 of the EU Taxonomy, as well as exposures supporting sustainable development, 
including sustainability -linked loans based on market standards for sustainab le financing: Sustainability -Linked Loan 
Principles; sustainability -linked bonds based on market standards for debt instruments: Sustainability -Linked Bond 
Principles; eco -friendly loans – including investment loans intended to finance investments in renew able energy 
sources, electromobility, energy -efficient real estate; and "Własny Kąt" mortgage loans for residential buildings that 
meet the criteria set out in the Green Covered Bond Framework. Quantitative data regarding products supporting 
sustainable de velopment are presented in the "Capital Adequacy and Other Information of the PKO Bank Polski S.A. 
Capital Group to be Published as of the Reporting Date 31 December 2023 and 31 December 2024 (Template 10 
Other climate change mitigation actions not covered  by Regulation (EU) 2020/852).

summary:
This section of PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 Director’s Report presents EU Taxonomy disclosures for climate-related objectives, detailing taxonomy-aligned economic activities by CapEx and Turnover using the mandatory templates.

- Scope and structure: Data are shown for both denominators (applicable KPI base) and numerators (taxonomy-aligned amounts) for CapEx and Turnover, split into climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), and total (CCM+CCA). Activities are categorized per Sections 4.26–4.31 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, with a residual “other taxonomy-aligned economic activities” category.

- Denominator (applicable KPI base):
  - CapEx: PLN 1,896m total (2.70%), largely CCM at PLN 1,869m (2.67%) with CCA PLN 27m (0.04%).
  - Turnover: PLN 1,822m total (2.60%), mostly CCM at PLN 1,797m (2.56%) with CCA PLN 24m (0.03%).
  - Minimal amounts are reported under Sections 4.27 and 4.28 (CapEx: PLN 2m and PLN 13m; Turnover: PLN 11m), with zero under 4.26 and 4.29–4.31. Most of the denominator is classified as “other taxonomy-aligned economic activities.”

- Numerator (taxonomy-aligned amounts):
  - CapEx: PLN 6,821m total (100%), dominated by CCM at PLN 6,763m (99.14%) and CCA at PLN 58m (0.86%). Small amounts under 4.27 (PLN 2m; 0.03%) and 4.28 (PLN 13m; 0.18%); none under 4.26 and 4.29–4.31. The bulk (PLN 6,806m; 99.78%) is “other taxonomy-aligned activities.”
  - Turnover: PLN 6,469m total (100%), mainly CCM at PLN 6,384m (98.69%) and CCA at PLN 85m (1.31%). Section 4.28 contributes PLN 11m (0.16%); zero under 4.26, 4.27, and 4.29–4.31. The majority (PLN 6,458m; 99.84%) is “other taxonomy-aligned activities.”

- Key takeaway: The Group’s taxonomy-aligned disclosures are overwhelmingly concentrated in climate change mitigation and primarily classified under “other taxonomy-aligned economic activities,” with only marginal amounts mapped to specific Sections 4.27–4.28 and none to 4.26 or 4.29–4.31.

Overall, the Group’s taxonomy-aligned CapEx and Turnover are overwhelmingly concentrated in “other” taxonomy-aligned activities rather than the specific sections 4.26–4.31, with the vast majority contributing to climate change mitigation and a small share to adaptation.

title: MATERIAL IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES AND THEIR INTERACTION WITH STRATEGY AND BUSINESS MODEL [E1.SBM-3] - Introduction
heading: MATERIAL IMPACTS , RISKS AND OPPORTUNI TIES AND THEIR INTER ACTION WITH STRATEGY AND BUSINESS MODEL [E1.SBM -3]
start_phrase: Climate risk, as a component of ESG risk, is assessed as a cross -cutting risk that may affect various types of risk within the Ban k in different ways, with a particularly significant impact on credit risk.
summary: Introduces PKO Bank Polski’s E1.SBM-3 framing of climate risk as a cross-cutting ESG risk managed within the bank’s broader risk management framework, with particularly significant impact on credit risk. Citing the Risk Management Strategy of PKO Bank Polski S.A. and Group, it defines ESG factors (environmental, social, governance; negative ones as ESG risk factors) and ESG risk (negative financial consequences for the bank from ESG factors affecting customers, counterparties, or balance sheet). For sustainability reporting and portfolio assessment, the bank adopts CRR III–aligned definitions of environmental physical risk (negative financial impacts from physical environmental factors) and transition risk (negative financial impacts from the transition to a sustainable economy) on counterparties and invested assets.
text:
MATERIAL IMPACTS , RISKS AND OPPORTUNI TIES AND THEIR INTER ACTION WITH STRATEGY  AND BUSINESS MODEL [E1.SBM -3] 
Climate risk, as a component of ESG risk, is assessed as a cross -cutting risk that may affect various types of risk 
within the Ban k in different ways, with a particularly significant impact on credit risk. Due to this characteristic, the 
Bank manages climate risk within the broader risk management framework.  
Definitions related to ESG risk are included in the “Risk Management Strate gy of PKO Bank Polski S.A. and the PKO 
Bank Polski S.A. Group”. They include:  
• ESG factors: environmental, social, and governance factors that may have a positive or negative impact on the 
Bank’s customers and counterparties or its balance sheet; ESG factor s with a negative impact are referred to as 
ESG risk factors;  
• ESG risk: the risk of negative financial consequences for the Bank of the current or future impact of ESG risk 
factors on customers and counterparties or the Bank’s statement of financial positi on items.  
For the purposes of sustainability reporting and portfolio assessment, the Bank adopts definitions of environmental 
(including climate -related) physical risk and transition risk in line with CRR III:  
• Physical risk, as a component of environmental  risk, refers to the risk of any negative financial consequences for 
an institution arising from the current or future impact of physical environmental factors on the institution’s 
counterparties or its invested assets;  
• Transition risk, as a component of e nvironmental risk, refers to the risk of any negative financial consequences 
for an institution arising from the current or future impact of the transition to an environmentally sustainable 
economy on the institution’s counterparties or its invested assets ;

title: Impact on the traditional types of risks
heading: Impact on the traditional types of risks
start_phrase: Credit Currency Interest rate Liquidity Operational Foreign currency mortgage loans Business Macroeconomic changes Models Reputational Insurance
summary:
- Focus on climate-related risks and ESG integration in PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s risk management, within the 2024 Director’s Report.
- Lists key transition risks and implementation challenges: materials/technology shortages for renewables, rising GHG allowance prices, new CO2/carbon tax regulations, building energy standards, need for low-emission tech investments, management gaps in CO2 reduction strategies, project execution inefficiencies, and social opposition to wind/solar near residential areas.
- Maps physical (acute: floods, hurricanes, heat waves; chronic: droughts, sea level rise) and transition risks (political/legal, technological, market, reputational, other) to traditional banking risk types, indicating identified and relative impact levels across credit, market, liquidity, operational, reputational, and insurance risks.
- Aligns risk assessment with Polish regulation (June 8, 2021) and expands 2024 materiality to include ESG/climate across credit, interest rate, liquidity/funding, FX, operational, reputational, compliance, and conduct risks.
- Liquidity/funding risk: recognizes direct ESG impact via access/cost of sustainable wholesale funding and indirect impact via stress-test deposit outflows (energy transition costs); incorporates ESG into internal capital methodology, with impact assessed as immaterial.
- Market risk: manages derivative risk via limits and stress testing; acknowledges potential ESG-related spread component in fair value corporate bonds, though current spread differentials between sustainable and other issues remain stably low.
- Notes that detailed climate risk management disclosures are provided separately in the Group’s Capital Adequacy report.
- Group entities’ ESG posture: participated in double materiality assessment; most are not yet standalone reporters or fully implementing IRO, but selected companies (PKO TU, PKO Życie) actively manage ESG/climate risks; PKO TFI applies Bloomberg ESG Score-based relative rankings and reports Principal Adverse Impact (PAI) indicators with sectoral breakdowns and data coverage.
- Climate stress testing: Bank developed a methodology based on ECB (2022) and NGFS scenarios; portfolio-level tests for the universal bank, with separate processes for insurance companies and plans to expand per evolving regulation.
- December 2024 stress test of the corporate (incl. specialized) portfolio covering 24% of exposure (mortgages excluded due to data limits) assessed physical risks (floods, droughts) and transition risks (GHG allowance price shocks, costs of low-carbon transition). Market and reputational transition risks were excluded due to quantification gaps.
- Scenario set spans acute flood (≤1 year), baseline and disorderly short-term GHG price paths (≤3 years), and long-term (2030/2040/2050) orderly, disorderly, and hot house world pathways, combining drought exposure, GHG prices, and transition investment assumptions.
- Key findings: limited physical risk impact (especially drought) on the corporate loan book; transition risks drive more material short- and long-term effects. Uncertainties include static portfolio assumptions and limits of NGFS/other forecasts.
- Application: results inform hypothetical ESG stress tests for determining the ESG-related credit spread component in fair value corporate bond portfolios and are intended for future integration into credit policy.
- Insurance subsidiaries (PKO TU, PKO Życie) executed PFSA-designed climate stress tests across five scenarios (including two to 2050), covering physical (hail, floods, hurricanes, higher mortality) and transition risks (equity price declines in high-emission sectors, price drops in energy-inefficient properties), aligned with NGFS Below 2°C and Hot House World pathways.

 The Bank also conducts an assessment of the materiality of traditional type s of banking risk in accordance with the 
Regulation of the Minister of Finance, Funds and Regional Policy of 8 June 2021 on the Risk Management System, 
the Internal Control System, and the Remuneration Policy. As part of this assessment, a catalogue of mat erial risks 
and risks subject to monitoring is established. As part of this assessment, a catalogue of material risks and risks 
subject to monitoring is established. The 2024 assessment incorporated the impact of ESG factors, with particular 
emphasis on cl imate risk factors, within the risk categories where the Bank identifies the potential materialisation of 
ESG risk, namely credit risk, interest rate risk, liquidity risk (including funding risk), foreign exchange risk, operational  
risk, reputational risk,  compliance risk, and conduct risk.  
With respect to liquidity and funding risk, the Bank considers ESG risk, including climate risk, as a risk factor that has 
both:  
• a direct impact – by factoring in additional costs arising from the inability to obtain su stainable financing in the 
wholesale market (which represents a lower -cost funding source) when rolling over or securing long -term 
funding sources;  
• an indirect impact – by incorporating ESG risk into stress -test deposit outflows (e.g. the effect of rising energy 
transition costs).  
ESG risk factors, including climate risk, have been incorporated into the methodology for determining internal capital 
requirements to cover this risk. The impact of ESG risk within liquidity risk on internal capital is assessed a s immaterial.  
As part of the market risk management process, the Bank identifies derivative risk, which is mitigated through the 
establishment of limits and thresholds as well as stress testing. In the area of market risk, current valuations of 
financial instruments do not indicate that transactions differ based on potential ESG aspects. However, within the 
portfolio of corporate bonds measured at fair value, an additional ESG risk -related spread component may be included 
based on the assessment of the ESG  profile of individual bond issuers. This ESG spread component (and its market 
volatility due to differing perceptions of issuers) may result in varying price fluctuations for specific debt instruments. 
The Bank’s analyses indicate a stable, low spread dif ferential between issuances supporting sustainable development 
and other debt instrument issuances.  
Detailed information on climate risk management is provided in the Report “Capital Adequacy and Other Information 
of the Powszechna Kasa Oszczędności Bank P olski Spółka Akcyjna Group Subject to Disclosure as at 31 December 
2024”.  
The Bank’s Group companies actively participated in the double materiality assessment process. However, at present, 
they are not subject to sustainability reporting obligations as st andalone entities and have not yet implemented 
individual internal procedures concerning IRO. They plan to undertake actions in this area in the future. Nevertheless, 
some of them (such as the previously mentioned PKO TU and PKO Życie) are already engaged in identifying and 
managing ESG risk, particularly climate risk, both within the Group and independently. PKO TFI conducts ESG risk 
assessments (in accordance with the provisions of the Investment Risk Management Policy) based on a relative ESG 
ranking ana lysis (according to Bloomberg’s methodology), calculated for each fund in comparison with the neutral 
ESG ranking level established for its benchmark or reference portfolio. The approach aims to monitor whether a fund 
adheres to its investment strategy and  sustainability risk policy in alignment with its benchmarks or reference 
portfolios. To this end, a synthetic ESG Score indicator, calculated and published by Bloomberg, is utilised (under this 
indicator, Bloomberg assesses how a company manages financial ly significant ESG risks, defined as risks that have 
a negative or positive financial impact on the company ). Additionally, PKO TFI considers Principal Adverse Impact 
indicators (PAIs) in its risk reporting. The report presents PAI indicators, including a breakdown by sectors that 
contribute most to individual indicator values, as well as information on data availability for each indicator as reported 
by issuers in the Bloomberg system.  
One of the analytical tools used to assess the resilience of credit portfolios to climate risks in financial institutions is 
climate stress testing. The Bank has developed its own climate stress -testing methodology, designed based on the 
standards set by the European Central Bank (hereinafter: ECB 2022), NGFS climate scena rios (NGFS – The Central 
Banks and Supervisors Network for Greening the Financial System, which voluntarily exchange experiences and best 
practices to develop environmental and climate risk management in the financial sector and to support the transition 
towards a sustainable economy ), and recognised publications on the materialisation of climate risk from the 
perspective of credit losses in financial institutions. This methodology enables the incorporation of a wide range of 
climate factors, provided they can be quantified from the perspective of customers' financial statements or variables 
used in credit risk models. The Bank conducts climate stress tests at the portfolio level for a universal bank portfolio. THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP  
DIRECTOR’S REPORT FOR 2024  
prepared jointly with the PKO Bank Polski S.A Director’s Report   
 
 Strona 240/288 
 
 
 A separate process has been carried out by PKO TU and PKO Życie concerning their insurance portfolios. The 
expansion of climate stress testing will be subject to further analysis in future periods, taking into account regulatory 
requirements.  
In December 2024, the Bank conducted a climate stress test o f its corporate credit portfolio, including specialised 
financing, covering 24% of the Bank's portfolio as of 31 December 2023. (The analysis does not include the mortgage 
loan portfolio due to limited data availability in this segment. The Bank is current ly analysing the impact of climate 
risk on LGD.) The analysis examined the impact of physical risk (droughts and floods) and transition risk (political 
and legal — changes in greenhouse gas emission allowance prices; technological — the costs of transition ing to low -
emission technologies) on customer rating assessments, as well as probability of default (PD) and expected credit 
loss (ECL) indicators.  Certain significant types of transition risk — market and reputational — were not included in the 
analysis due to the lack of quantification methods.

title: Impact of climate physical risk on the Bank's loan portfolio
heading: Table 81. Impact of climate physical risk on the Bank's loan portfolio
start_phrase: SCENARIO TIME HORIZON PHYSICAL RISKS TRANSITION RISKS DATA SOURCES GENERAL ASSUMPTIONS
summary:
- Focus: Climate risk management and transition planning within PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group, covering stress testing of banking and insurance portfolios, key findings, limitations, and the Group’s newly adopted Transition Plan.

- Bank climate stress testing (Dec 2024):
  - Scope: Corporate credit portfolio (incl. specialised financing), 24% of portfolio as of 31 Dec 2023; mortgages excluded due to data gaps; LGD climate impact under analysis.
  - Risks/modeling: Physical (floods, droughts) and transition (policy/legal via GHG allowance prices; technology transition costs). Market and reputational transition risks not quantified.
  - Scenarios: Acute flood (≤1 year); near-term baseline and disorderly (≤3 years) driven by GHG price paths; long-term NGFS-based Orderly, Disorderly, and Hot House World (2030/2040/2050) with differing policy timing, warming limits, and risk balances.
  - Results: Limited physical risk impact (especially prolonged drought) on the corporate portfolio; transition risks materially affect ratings, PD, and ECL in both short and long term.
  - Uncertainties: Static portfolio assumption; limitations of NGFS and other forecasts.
  - Use of results: Feeding hypothetical ESG stress tests to attribute an ESG credit spread for corporate bonds at FV; planned integration into credit policy.

- Insurance stress testing (PKO TU and PKO Życie):
  - Conducted per PFSA Office methodology; five qualitative/quantitative scenarios incl. two to 2050; physical (hail, floods, hurricanes, mortality) and transition (equity declines in high-emission sectors, price drops of energy-inefficient properties).
  - Long-term assumptions aligned with NGFS Below 2°C and Hot House World.
  - Outcomes: No breach of SCR/MCR; results embedded in risk management, planning, product decisions, reinsurance structures, investment strategy, and financial plans.

- Gaps/limitations:
  - No assessment of the Group’s ability to align strategy/business model to climate change across time horizons.
  - Upstream value chain risks not included in resilience analysis.

- Transition Plan for climate change mitigation (adopted 24 Feb 2025):
  - Aim: Support Paris Agreement 1.5°C goal; cover own operations and financed emissions (scope 3).
  - Targets/objectives: Net-zero by 2050; reduce scope 1–2 emissions and source ≥90% renewable energy; improve building energy efficiency; support customer energy efficiency (scope 3).
  - Initial focus: Set scope 1–2 targets for the Bank first (Bank = 75.6% of Group emissions; Ukrainian subs ~5% constrained by wartime; remaining 19.4% are Polish subs, some in Bank-owned buildings).
  - Loan portfolio prioritization: Based on environmental impact (exposure share and emissions intensity), sector decarbonisation potential (policy/programs, economics, barriers), and market practices/tools.
  - Priority sectors selected: Energy generation and residential real estate (residential targets for PKO Bank Polski S.A. and PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A.; energy generation for the Bank). These sectors represent >42% of the Group’s loan portfolio by gross carrying amount.
  - Next steps: Refine financed-emissions methodologies, improve data quality, and expand sectoral targets over time; periodic plan review and scope expansion.

summary: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s Management Board adopted its Transition Plan on 24 Feb 2025 to align with the Paris Agreement 1.5°C goal, covering both own operations (Scopes 1–2) and financed emissions (Scope 3 loan portfolio). The Plan targets net-zero by 2050, ≥90% renewable energy sourcing, improved building energy efficiency, and support for customers’ energy efficiency. Initial targets focus on the Bank, which generates 75.6% of Group emissions (Ukrainian subsidiaries 5% under wartime constraints; Polish subsidiaries 19.4%, some in Bank-owned properties benefiting from building measures). Priority lending sectors were selected via analysis of portfolio share and emissions intensity per PLN 1m, the Group’s national emissions financing share, sector decarbonization potential (policies, programs, economic and legal/technological factors), and market practices/tools. Energy generation (targets apply to the Bank) and residential real estate (targets apply to PKO Bank Polski S.A. and PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A.) were chosen first, covering over 42% of the Group’s gross loan portfolio. text:
TRANSITION PLAN FOR C LIMATE CHANGE MITIGA TION [E1-1] 
On 24 February 2025, the Management Board of the Bank adopted the "Transition Plan of the PKO Bank Polski S.A. 
Group" aimed at supporting the achievement of the long -term objective of the Paris Agreement —making efforts to 
limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre -industrial levels. The Plan sets out goals and actions concerning 
both the Bank’s own operations and the financed emissions of the Bank’s Group (scope 3 – loan portfolio).  
The Transition Plan contributes to the achievement of strategic sus tainability objectives:  
• achieving net -zero by 2050;  
• reducing own emissions (scope 1 and 2) and sourcing at least 90% of energy from renewable sources;  
• improving the energy efficiency of buildings;  
• supporting customers in enhancing energy efficiency (scope  3). 
For the targets related to the Bank’s own operations (scope 1 and 2, in line with the Strategy), it was decided to set 
them first for the Bank. The Bank's emissions account for 75.6% of the Group’s total emissions. A further 5% is 
generated by Ukraini an subsidiaries, which operate under wartime conditions and utilise available fuel and energy 
resources regardless of their emissions intensity. The remaining 19.4% of the Group’s emissions originate from Polish 
subsidiaries, some of which are located in p roperties owned by the Bank. This means that any measures taken by the 
Bank to reduce the emissions of the buildings it uses will also indirectly contribute to reducing the emissions of these 
subsidiaries. Limiting the initial scope of the Transition Plan to the Bank’s own emissions aligns with the current 
Strategy’s objectives.  
The setting of targets for the loan portfolio was preceded by an analysis aimed at identifying the sectors to be 
prioritised in the Transition Plan. The selection of priority secto rs was based on the assumptions of the 2025 –2027 
Strategy and took into account factors such as:  
• the scale of the Group’s environmental impact, measured as the share of financing for a given sector in the loan 
portfolio (based on gross carrying amount) and  the emissions intensity of the financed activity per PLN 1 million 
of financing provided. The analysis also considered the Group’s share in financing emissions at the national level;  
• the decarbonisation potential of the sector, which included national tr ansition priorities, existing and planned 
regulations and programmes supporting decarbonisation in the sector, economic conditions, and potential legal 
and technological barriers;  
• market practices in setting GHG reduction targets for specific sectors by fi nancial institutions, including the 
availability of sector -specific decarbonisation pathways and tools.  
From a shortlist of several industries, the energy generation sector and the residential real estate sector were selected 
as the starting points for set ting greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets related to lending activities. The targets 
for the residential real estate sector apply to two Group entities providing such loans (PKO Bank Polski S.A. and PKO 
Bank Hipoteczny S.A.), while the targets for th e energy generation sector apply to the Bank. Further work is planned 
to refine the methodologies for calculating financed emissions, improve the quality of emissions data, and expand 
the targets to additional key sectors.  
The selection process initially f ocused on companies and exposures generating the highest emissions. Exposures to 
the two selected sectors account for over 42% of the gross carrying amount of the Bank Group’s loan portfolio. The 
Transition Plan will be reviewed and gradually expanded in s cope.  
THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP  
DIRECTOR’S REPORT FOR 2024  
prepared jointly with the PKO Bank Polski S.A Director’s Report   
 
 Strona 242/288 
 
 
 Actions have been planned for 2025 –2027 in line with the Strategy adopted by the Bank. Given the early stage of 
implementing the Transition Plan, full allocation of financial and other resources for the planned initiatives has not 
yet been completed .
